01_Recognising_chemical_change.json.title: Recognising chemical change
01_Recognising_chemical_change.json.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Classify a described or depicted change as physical or chemical by comparing the particles present before and after the change, not by surface appearance alone.
Evaluate a piece of evidence (colour change, bubbles, temperature change, dissolving) and decide whether it is, on its own, sufficient proof that a chemical change has occurred.

prerequisites.statement: A substance can exist as a solid, liquid or gas, and can change between these states by heating or cooling.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A change of state is the main physical change learners meet first, and it must already feel 'reversible and ordinary' before it can be contrasted with a chemical change.

prerequisites.statement: A compound is made of two or more elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio, shown by its formula.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Deciding whether a 'new substance' has formed means comparing formulae/compositions before and after, which only makes sense once a compound's fixed composition is understood.

diagnostic_items.question: Liquid water is cooled until it freezes into ice. Has a new substance been formed?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. The ice is still water, $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$; only the arrangement and movement of the particles have changed, not their composition.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, because ice and water look and behave differently (one is hard, one flows).
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is classifying by physical appearance/behaviour rather than by checking whether the particles themselves have changed.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It cannot be decided without a chemical test.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has not yet connected 'change of state' to 'same particles, no new bonds', and treats every outcome as needing fresh evidence rather than applying what they already know about freezing.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner can apply the prerequisite ('a substance can change state') to conclude, without any new evidence, that no new substance has formed.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner to write the formula of the substance before and after freezing; since the formula $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ does not change, no new substance can have been formed, whatever the solid looks or feels like.

theory_blocks.title: Two kinds of 'different'
theory_blocks.body:
Melt an ice cube and you get a puddle of water: clearly different from the ice to look at, yet still exactly the same substance.

Burn a strip of magnesium ribbon and you get a crumbly white ash: also clearly different to look at, but this time a genuinely new substance has appeared, one that did not exist before the burning started.

Both changes look dramatic. Both change how the material behaves. The question that actually separates them is not 'did it look different afterwards?' but 'are the particles present after the change [[blue:the same particles,

just rearranged]], or are they [[orange:new particles bonded in a new way]]?' Everything in this lesson comes down to answering that one question with evidence, not with a guess based on appearance.

theory_blocks.title: Defining physical and chemical change by composition
theory_blocks.body:
- A **physical change** rearranges, mixes or changes the state of particles without breaking or making chemical bonds. The substances present before the change are exactly the substances present after it: melting, freezing, boiling, condensing, dissolving and most forms of mixing (mixing sand and water, mixing two unreactive powders) are physical.
- A **chemical change** (a chemical reaction) breaks bonds in the starting substances (reactants) and makes new bonds, so that at least one new substance (a product), with its own new formula and new properties, is formed. Burning, rusting, a precipitate forming, and a fizzing reaction between an acid and a metal are chemical.

The test is always the same: compare the formula/composition of what is present before the change with what is present after. If nothing new appears, however different it looks or feels, the change is physical.

The figure below places a physical change and a chemical change side by side so the composition, not the appearance, decides the category.

assets.caption: Top: ice melting to water keeps the same four $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ particles, just rearranged (physical). Bottom: magnesium burning in oxygen ($2\mathrm{Mg}+\mathrm{O_{2}}\rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}$) forms a new bonded substance, magnesium oxide, that did not exist before (chemical).
assets.purpose: Lets a learner apply the composition test directly to a physical and a chemical change built from the same number of starting atoms, so only bonding and identity, not atom count, can explain the difference.

theory_blocks.title: Evidence is a clue, not a verdict
theory_blocks.body:
Bubbles, a colour change, or a temperature change are all common signs that a chemical reaction might be happening, and in an exam you are expected to use them.

But each one can also appear during a purely physical change: boiling water makes bubbles of steam; diluting a coloured solution changes its colour; evaporation cools the surroundings slightly.

The evidence narrows down what to check, but the verdict always comes from the same test as before — has a new substance, with a new composition, actually appeared?

theory_blocks.title: When the same evidence has two explanations

keywords.definition: A change that rearranges, mixes or alters the state of particles, without breaking or forming chemical bonds, so no new substance is produced.
A change in which bonds break and new bonds form, producing at least one new substance with a new composition and new properties.
A starting substance that is chemically changed during a reaction.
A new substance formed as the result of a chemical reaction.
An insoluble solid that forms and settles out when two solutions react together.

worked_examples.statement: **Three everyday changes.** Classify each as physical or chemical: (a) ice cubes melting in a drink, (b) a slice of bread toasting until brown and crisp, (c) sugar dissolving in a cup of tea.
solution: (a) Melting only rearranges the $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ particles already present; the ice and the melted water are the same substance, so this is **physical**.
(b) Toasting bread involves heat-driven chemical reactions in the starches and sugars that produce new brown, crisp compounds that were not present in the original bread; this is **chemical**.
(c) Dissolving spreads sugar particles through the tea without forming new bonds; the sugar can in principle be recovered unchanged by evaporating the tea, so this is **physical**.
worked_examples.interpretation: Toasting is the deliberately tricky case here: it looks like a simple physical heating, but new substances (giving the new colour, smell and texture) are actually formed, which is exactly what makes it chemical.

worked_examples.statement: **Rusting iron.** A clean iron nail left outdoors slowly becomes covered in a flaky orange-brown layer, and the nail itself becomes measurably lighter and more brittle in that spot over time. Decide whether rusting is physical or chemical, and justify your answer using composition.
solution: The orange-brown layer (rust, mainly hydrated iron oxide) has a different composition from iron: it contains oxygen (from the air) and water chemically combined with the iron, which plain iron metal does not.
Because a new substance, with a different formula and different properties (flaky, brittle, no longer metallic-shiny) from the original iron, has appeared, this is a **chemical** change.

The surface colour change and change in texture are evidence that prompted the investigation, but the decisive point is that the composition of the surface material has changed, not simply its appearance.
worked_examples.interpretation: Rusting is a slow reaction, which is useful precisely because it shows that 'chemical' does not require a fast or dramatic change; the composition test applies regardless of speed.

worked_examples.statement: **An ambiguous colour change.** Blue copper(II) sulfate solution is split into two test tubes. To tube 1, more water is added, and the blue colour becomes paler. To tube 2, sodium hydroxide solution is added, and a pale blue solid forms and settles at the bottom, while the solution above it becomes almost colourless. A student says 'both tubes show a colour change, so both must be chemical reactions.' Evaluate this claim.
solution: The student is using 'colour changed' as the whole test, but colour change on its own is not proof of a chemical change (as seen with dilution).
In tube 1, only water has been added; no new substance has formed, and the same dissolved copper(II) sulfate is simply more spread out, which is why it looks paler — this is **physical**.

In tube 2, a new solid (copper(II) hydroxide) has appeared that was not present in either starting solution, and it has different properties (insoluble, settles out) from both; a new substance has formed, so this is **chemical**.
The student's claim is wrong for tube 1 and happens to be right for tube 2, but for the wrong reason (colour change, rather than new-substance formation).
worked_examples.interpretation: This pins down exactly where the misconception breaks: the same surface evidence (a colour change) sits on top of two different underlying facts, and only checking for a new substance tells them apart.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating 'the colour changed' as sufficient justification, without separately checking whether a new substance (here, the solid precipitate) actually appeared.

worked_examples.statement: **Baking a cake.** Describe at least one physical change and one chemical change that happen while a cake batter is baked in an oven, and explain how you know which is which.
solution: Physical change: the butter in the batter melts and the sugar dissolves in the liquid, so the mixture becomes more runny before it sets; melting and dissolving only rearrange particles already present (butter stays butter, sugar stays sugar at this stage) without forming new substances.

Chemical change: a raising agent such as baking powder reacts on heating to release carbon dioxide gas, which was not simply dissolved beforehand but is produced as a new substance by a reaction inside the batter; separately, proteins and sugars on the surface undergo browning reactions that form new brown-coloured compounds (similar in kind to toasting bread).

The distinguishing test is the same as always: melting only rearranges existing particles, while gas production from a raising agent and surface browning both produce substances (carbon dioxide gas, new brown compounds) that were not present in the raw batter.
worked_examples.interpretation: Baking packs a physical and a chemical change into the same familiar process, which is exactly the kind of transfer a learner needs to be able to unpick outside a laboratory context.

guided_exercises.statement: Silver nitrate solution is colourless. When it is added to colourless sodium chloride solution, a white solid cloudiness (precipitate) appears immediately. Decide whether this is a physical or a chemical change, and justify your answer.
hints: Start by listing what substances are present before the mixing: two colourless solutions.
Now ask: is the white solid one of the substances that was already present, or does it have a composition that neither starting solution had on its own?
A new solid appearing from two clear solutions, with different properties from either, is a strong signal worth checking against the composition test.
guided_exercises.answer: This is a **chemical** change. The white solid (silver chloride) is a new substance, insoluble in water, that was not present in either the silver nitrate solution or the sodium chloride solution before mixing; its formation shows that new chemical bonds have formed between silver and chloride ions that were previously bonded to different partners.
common_errors: Assuming that because both starting solutions are 'just salts dissolved in water', nothing chemical can be happening, without checking whether the solid product is actually one of the original dissolved substances.

guided_exercises.statement: A student dissolves copper(II) sulfate crystals in water to make a blue solution, then evaporates the water completely and recovers blue copper(II) sulfate crystals of the same mass as before. Explain what this recovery shows about whether dissolving was a chemical change.
hints: Compare the substance before dissolving (crystals) with the substance recovered after evaporating (crystals): are they the same substance?
If dissolving had been a chemical change, what would you expect to be left behind after evaporation?
Think about what 'recovering the same mass of the same substance, unchanged' tells you about whether any new bonds were ever formed.
guided_exercises.answer: Because the same copper(II) sulfate, with the same mass, same colour and same composition, is recovered after evaporation, no new substance was ever formed and no chemical bond was broken or made; dissolving only separated the copper(II) sulfate particles and spread them through the water, which is a **physical** change. If dissolving had been chemical, evaporation would be expected to leave behind a different substance, not the original copper(II) sulfate.
common_errors: Describing the dissolved copper(II) sulfate as having 'turned into' the solution, rather than as still being present as separate, spread-out particles.

exercises.statement: Classify each of the following changes as physical or chemical, giving one reason based on composition for each: (a) candle wax melting near a flame, (b) the same candle wax burning at the wick to produce soot, water vapour and carbon dioxide, (c) ice cream melting on a warm day, (d) a firework exploding to produce coloured light, smoke and new solid residues.
exercises.answer: (a) Physical: the melted wax is still the same wax, just a liquid instead of a solid; no new substance appears. (b) Chemical: burning wax produces soot, water vapour and carbon dioxide, none of which was present in the solid wax, so new substances have formed. (c) Physical: melted ice cream is still the same mixture of ingredients, only rearranged by melting. (d) Chemical: the explosive reaction produces light-emitting gases and new solid residues that were not present in the unlit firework's chemicals.

exercises.statement: A student adds a few drops of universal indicator to a colourless solution and sees the indicator turn from green to red. Does this colour change, on its own, prove that the colourless solution is acidic because a chemical reaction has happened? Explain your reasoning.
exercises.answer: The colour change is strong evidence that the solution is acidic, but the chemical change here is in the indicator dye itself (which is designed to change colour reversibly in response to acidity), not necessarily evidence that a brand-new permanent substance has been formed in the original solution. The colour change is a useful, reliable signal in this specific case because universal indicator is built for exactly this purpose, but 'colour changed' is still not, by itself, a general proof of chemical change without knowing what is producing the colour change.
common_errors: Treating every colour change as equally strong evidence, rather than considering what is known about the specific substance (here, an indicator) causing it.

exercises.statement: Limestone (calcium carbonate) is heated strongly and breaks down into quicklime (calcium oxide) and carbon dioxide gas. Explain why this is a chemical change, naming the evidence you would look for and the composition argument that confirms it.
exercises.answer: Evidence to look for: a gas is given off (carbon dioxide can be tested with limewater, which turns cloudy) and the solid remaining (quicklime) looks and behaves differently from the original limestone (it reacts vigorously with water, unlike limestone). The composition argument: calcium carbonate, $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}$, has broken apart into two different substances, calcium oxide, $\mathrm{CaO}$, and carbon dioxide, $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$, neither of which has the same formula as the original limestone; because new substances with new formulae have appeared, this is a chemical change, not merely a physical one.

exercises.statement: A bottle of fizzy drink is opened and bubbles rise to the surface; separately, a tablet of indigestion remedy is dropped into a glass of water and bubbles rise to the surface. Explain why the same observation (bubbles rising) can have two different explanations, and state what further evidence would distinguish the two cases.
exercises.answer: In the fizzy drink, carbon dioxide gas was already dissolved in the liquid under pressure; opening the bottle simply lets the existing gas escape, which is a physical change (no new substance is formed). In the indigestion tablet, the tablet's ingredients (commonly a carbonate and a weak acid) react together when they dissolve, producing carbon dioxide gas as a genuinely new substance that was not present, dissolved or otherwise, before the tablet touched the water; this is a chemical change. The two cases could be distinguished by checking the composition of the materials before and after: the fizzy drink's dissolved gas leaves the drink's other ingredients completely unchanged, while the tablet's ingredients are used up and replaced by new substances in the solution.

exercises.statement: Define the key terms used in the study of 'Recognising chemical change'.
exercises.answer: Key definitions should cover the main concepts from 'Recognising chemical change' using precise scientific language.

exercises.statement: Explain one key concept from 'Recognising chemical change' and give a real-world example.
exercises.answer: A full answer should clearly explain the concept using correct terminology and link it to a practical everyday example.

exam_questions.statement: A student heats blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals gently. The crystals turn into a white powder, and droplets of liquid collect on the cooler part of the test tube. When water is later added back to the white powder, it turns blue again and becomes warm. State, with a reason, whether heating the hydrated crystals is a physical or a chemical change.
exam_questions.answer: It is a **chemical** change. Hydrated copper(II) sulfate, $\mathrm{CuSO_{4}{\cdot}5H_{2}O}$, contains water *chemically combined* in its crystals. Heating breaks these bonds and forms two new substances with different formulae and properties: white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, $\mathrm{CuSO_{4}}$, and water (the droplets). Adding water back forms new bonds again, and the heat given out (the powder becomes warm) is further evidence of a chemical reaction. The fact that the change can be reversed does not make it physical: it is a **reversible reaction**, $\mathrm{CuSO_{4}{\cdot}5H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons CuSO_{4} + 5H_{2}O}$.
mark_scheme: States that the change is chemical / a (reversible) chemical reaction.
Water is chemically combined (bonded) in the hydrated crystals.
Heating forms new substances with different formulae/properties: (white) anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water.
Reversibility does not make it physical: it is a reversible reaction, and the heat given out on adding water shows new bonds forming.

exam_questions.statement: Magnesium ribbon is burned in air. Before burning, the ribbon has a mass of 0.24 g. After burning, all of the magnesium has reacted and the solid product (magnesium oxide) has a mass of 0.40 g. Explain, using this mass change, why burning magnesium is a chemical change, and explain why the mass of the solid increased even though nothing was added by hand.
exam_questions.answer: The solid product has a different mass (0.40 g) from the starting magnesium (0.24 g), and a different formula: magnesium oxide, $\mathrm{MgO}$, is not the same substance as magnesium metal, $\mathrm{Mg}$, so a new substance has clearly formed, which makes this a chemical change. The mass increased because magnesium atoms bonded with oxygen atoms taken from the surrounding air; no mass was added 'by hand', but oxygen from the air became chemically combined into the solid product, so the solid's mass is the combined mass of the original magnesium plus the oxygen it reacted with, which is why the total mass of the solid product is greater than the mass of magnesium alone.
mark_scheme: States that the product has a different formula/identity from the starting magnesium.
Concludes that a new substance has formed, so the change is chemical.
Explains that the extra mass comes from oxygen taken from the air, not created from nothing.
States that this oxygen becomes chemically bonded to the magnesium in the solid product.
Does not claim that mass has been created or destroyed overall.

challenge_questions.statement:
Both of the changes below can be undone.

- **A** Solid iodine is warmed gently in a test tube. It turns straight into a purple vapour, and grey crystals of iodine re-form on the cool upper walls of the tube.
- **B** Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals are heated. They turn into a white powder, and droplets of liquid collect on the cooler part of the tube. When water is added to the white powder it turns blue again and the tube becomes warm.

Classify each change as physical or chemical, justifying each decision by composition rather than by the fact that it can be undone, and state what this pair of changes shows about the rule 'if a change can be reversed, it must be physical'.
hints: For each change, ask what substance is present at the start and what substances are present at the end; write their formulae if you can.
In **B**, where could the droplets of liquid have come from, if the blue crystals were a dry solid to begin with?
Heat given out is a clue about bonds: breaking bonds takes energy in, making bonds gives energy out.
challenge_questions.answer:
**A is physical.** The purple vapour and the grey crystals are both iodine, $\mathrm{I_{2}}$: the molecules are unchanged and only their arrangement and spacing differ, so no new substance has formed. (Solid turning straight into vapour is sublimation, and the vapour turning straight back into solid on the cold glass is deposition.)

**B is chemical.** The blue crystals are hydrated copper(II) sulfate, $\mathrm{CuSO_{4}{\cdot}5H_{2}O}$, in which the water is *chemically combined*. Heating breaks those bonds and gives two substances with different formulae and properties: white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, $\mathrm{CuSO_{4}}$, and water (the droplets). Adding water forms those bonds again, and the heat given out is further evidence of new bonds forming. Written as an equation, $\mathrm{CuSO_{4}{\cdot}5H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons CuSO_{4} + 5H_{2}O}$.

Both changes can be reversed, yet only one of them forms new substances, so 'reversible' cannot be the test. **B** is a [[blue:reversible chemical reaction]], not a physical change. The test is always the same: compare the substances present before and after, and ask whether any new substance has been formed.
common_errors: Classifying **B** as physical because the blue colour can be brought back, instead of checking whether the white powder and the droplets are new substances.
Calling **A** chemical because the purple vapour looks nothing like the grey solid, which is a judgement by appearance rather than by composition.

challenge_questions.statement:
A student performs four experiments and observes: (i) a colour change from orange to green, (ii) fizzing when a tablet is dropped in water, (iii) a white precipitate forming when two solutions are mixed, (iv) ice melting.
(a) State which observations indicate a chemical change and which indicate a physical change. (2 marks)
(b) For each chemical change, suggest a possible reaction that could produce the observation. (3 marks)
(c) Explain why the formation of gas bubbles alone is not sufficient proof of a chemical reaction. (1 mark)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Chemical changes: (i), (ii) and (iii). Physical change: (iv).
(b) (i) Acidified potassium dichromate reduced by an alcohol — orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ turns green Cr³⁺. (ii) An antacid tablet reacting with water/acid to produce CO₂. (iii) Mixing silver nitrate with sodium chloride to precipitate silver chloride.
(c) Bubbles can be produced by physical processes such as boiling or dissolved gas escaping from a liquid when pressure is released. Therefore, fizzing alone does not confirm a chemical reaction.

mcq.stem: Which change is physical rather than chemical?

options.text: A strip of magnesium burning brightly in air to form a white powder
options.why_wrong: the white powder, magnesium oxide, has a different formula from magnesium metal, so a new substance has formed.

options.text: Steam condensing on a cold window to form liquid water droplets
Iron nails rusting over several weeks outdoors
options.why_wrong: rust has a different composition (it includes oxygen and water chemically combined with iron) from the original iron.

options.text: A firework exploding to leave behind new coloured solid residues
options.why_wrong: new solid residues with different compositions from the firework's original chemicals have been formed.

mcq.explanation: Condensation only rearranges the same $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ particles from gas to liquid; no new substance is formed, so it is purely physical.

mcq.stem: A student sees bubbles forming when a tablet is dropped into water and says 'this proves a chemical reaction is happening.' Which statement best evaluates this claim?

options.text: The claim is always correct, because bubbles can only be produced by a chemical reaction.
options.why_wrong: bubbles can also appear when a gas that was already dissolved, such as in a fizzy drink, simply escapes without any new substance forming.

options.text: The claim is always wrong, because bubbles are never evidence of a chemical reaction.
options.why_wrong: bubbles very often are produced by a genuine chemical reaction, such as a carbonate reacting with an acid; the issue is that bubbles alone are not a complete proof.

options.text: Bubbles are a useful clue, but whether a reaction has really happened still needs to be confirmed by checking for a new substance.
The claim cannot be evaluated without knowing the colour of the bubbles.
options.why_wrong: the colour of bubbles is not a relevant or usable piece of evidence for deciding between a physical and a chemical change.

mcq.explanation: Bubbles are suggestive evidence (as with a carbonate-acid reaction), but the decisive test is always whether a genuinely new substance, with a new composition, has been formed.

mcq.stem: Sugar is stirred into hot tea until it completely disappears from view. Which statement correctly classifies this change?

options.text: It is chemical, because the sugar has completely disappeared and cannot be seen.
options.why_wrong: the sugar particles are still present, just spread out and too small to see individually; nothing has to have reacted just because it is no longer visible.

options.text: It cannot be classified without testing the sugar's melting point first.
options.why_wrong: a melting-point test is unnecessary here; the recoverability of the unchanged sugar already settles the question.

options.text: It is chemical, because dissolving always involves breaking chemical bonds within the solid.
options.why_wrong: dissolving breaks only the weaker attractions holding the solid's particles to each other, not the chemical bonds inside each sugar particle itself.

options.text: It is physical, because the same sugar can be recovered unchanged, for example by evaporating the tea.

mcq.explanation: Dissolved sugar particles are still sugar, just spread through the tea; since the same sugar can be recovered unchanged, no new substance has been formed and the change is physical.

mcq.stem: Which pair of observations, taken together, gives the strongest evidence that a chemical change has happened, rather than only a physical one?

options.text: A new solid formed that is insoluble, where both starting substances were soluble solutions.
The substance became paler in colour and slightly warmer.
options.why_wrong: both a colour fading and a small temperature change can occur during purely physical processes, such as dilution or evaporation.

options.text: The substance changed from a solid to a liquid and took up more space.
options.why_wrong: melting and expanding on melting are typical physical changes, with the same substance present throughout.

options.text: The substance's temperature dropped as it was stirred into water.
options.why_wrong: many purely physical processes, such as some substances dissolving, absorb energy from their surroundings and cool them, without any new substance forming.

mcq.explanation: An insoluble solid appearing from two soluble starting solutions is strong evidence of a new substance with new properties, which is exactly the composition test for a chemical change.

flashcards.front: What is a physical change?
flashcards.back: A change that rearranges, mixes or changes the state of particles without breaking or making chemical bonds; the same substances are present before and after.

flashcards.front: What is a chemical change?
flashcards.back: A change in which bonds in the reactants break and new bonds form, so that at least one new substance, with a new formula and new properties, is produced.

flashcards.front: Dissolving salt in water versus a precipitate forming when two solutions are mixed: which is physical and which is chemical, and why?
flashcards.back: Dissolving salt is physical: the same salt can be recovered unchanged by evaporation. A precipitate forming is chemical: a new, different (often insoluble) substance appears that was not present in either starting solution.

flashcards.front: A solution changes colour when diluted with water. Does this prove a chemical reaction has happened?
flashcards.back: No. Colour change on its own is not proof; dilution is a physical change that spreads the same particles further apart, which can make a colour look paler without any new substance forming.

flashcards.front: Ice melts into water, which is later refrozen into ice. What does this show about whether melting is a chemical change?
flashcards.back: Because the exact same substance reappears on refreezing, no new substance was ever formed and no chemical bond was broken; melting (and freezing) are physical changes.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any colour change on its own proves that a chemical reaction has happened.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners' first vivid reaction demonstrations (a dramatic colour flash) wire 'colour change' and 'chemical reaction' together, and no counter-example is offered at the same time.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says a reaction 'must' have happened purely because a colour changed, without checking whether a new substance was actually formed.
misconceptions.correct_model: A colour change can be caused by a chemical reaction (iron rusting, a precipitate forming), but it can also be purely physical (a solution becoming more dilute and paler, or a solid dissolving and losing its surface colour); colour change is a clue to look further, not proof by itself.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare diluting blue copper(II) sulfate solution with water (paler blue, same substance, physical) against adding sodium hydroxide solution to the same copper(II) sulfate solution (a new blue solid precipitate forms, chemical); ask what composition test would tell the two apart.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Dissolving a solid in a liquid is always a chemical reaction, because the solid 'disappears'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The solid visibly vanishes into the liquid, which feels like the dramatic disappearance learners associate with a substance being used up in a reaction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes dissolved salt as 'gone' or 'changed into water', rather than as still present but spread out as separate particles too small to see.
misconceptions.correct_model: Dissolving is a physical change: the solid's particles separate and mix with the liquid's particles, but no new chemical bonds form and the dissolved substance can usually be recovered unchanged (for example, by evaporating the water).
misconceptions.remediation: Dissolve salt in water, then evaporate the water and show that the same mass of the same salt reappears, with the same taste and melting point; ask what this recovery shows about whether a new substance had been formed.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A change of state (melting, freezing, boiling, condensing) changes the chemical composition of a substance.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Melting and boiling look dramatic and are often taught alongside chemical reactions in the same 'things that happen when you heat stuff' category, without the composition test being made explicit.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says that steam is 'different' from water in composition, or that melted wax is a new substance because it now flows.
misconceptions.correct_model: A change of state only changes how particles are arranged and how much energy they have; the chemical formula and the bonds within each particle stay the same, so no new substance is formed, however different the solid, liquid and gas look or behave.
misconceptions.remediation: Melt an ice cube, then refreeze the water, and ask the learner to write the formula of the substance at every stage; since the formula never changes, the composition has not changed either.

common_mistakes.mistake: Classifying a change as chemical purely because a colour, temperature or state changed.
common_mistakes.why: Dramatic physical changes (dilution, evaporation, melting) can produce the same visible signals as a chemical reaction.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always finish by asking whether a substance with a genuinely new composition has appeared; if not, the change is physical however dramatic it looked.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating dissolving as automatically chemical because the solid 'disappears'.
common_mistakes.why: The solid becomes invisible, which feels like the same kind of disappearance as a reactant being used up in a reaction.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check whether the original substance could be recovered unchanged (for example, by evaporation); if it can, nothing new was ever formed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a change of state alters a substance's chemical composition.
common_mistakes.why: Melting, freezing, boiling and condensing look like transformations, which blurs the distinction between a physical rearrangement and a chemical change of identity.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the formula of the substance before and after the change of state; if the formula is unchanged, the composition has not changed.

exam_notes: When asked to classify a change, always state the composition evidence explicitly (name the new substance formed, or state that the same substance is recoverable), rather than only naming the category.

Reversibility by a simple physical method (evaporation, cooling, melting back) is good supporting evidence for a physical change, but is not by itself the definition: some chemical reactions are reversible too (for example, hydrated copper(II) sulfate losing and regaining water). The definition is always about whether a new substance has formed.
A single piece of evidence (colour, bubbles, temperature) is rarely enough on an exam answer; name the evidence and then state what it does or does not prove about composition.

summary.big_idea: A change is chemical only if it produces a new substance with a new composition; appearance alone (colour, bubbles, temperature, state) is evidence to investigate, never proof by itself.
key_points: Physical changes rearrange existing particles (melting, dissolving, mixing); the same substances are present before and after.
Chemical changes break and form bonds, producing at least one genuinely new substance that did not exist before.
Colour change, bubbles and temperature change can each occur in both physical and chemical changes, so none of them alone is decisive.
The decisive test is always composition: compare what substances are present before the change with what is present after it.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Ask 'has a new substance appeared?' before deciding chemical or physical; never decide from appearance alone.

exit_check.question: A student dissolves a coloured solid in water, and the solution has a paler colour than the solid. They claim this proves a chemical reaction. Is the student's reasoning sound?
exit_check.answer: No. A paler colour after dissolving is typical of a physical change, because the same coloured particles are simply spread out through the water; unless a new substance with a different composition can be shown to have formed, colour change alone does not prove a reaction.

02_Measuring_rate_and_testing_factors.js.title: Measuring rate and testing factors
02_Measuring_rate_and_testing_factors.js.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Calculate the mean rate of a reaction over a time interval from measured data (gas volume produced or mass lost), and interpret the gradient of a volume/mass-time graph as the rate at that point.
Design and justify a fair (controlled) test for a rate factor, choosing one independent variable, stating the variables that must be controlled, and choosing a suitable measurable signal.

Compare two volume/mass-time graphs that reach the same final value and identify which reaction was faster from the steepness of the early gradient, correctly distinguishing rate from the final amount of product.

prerequisites.statement: A balanced symbol equation names the reactants and products of a reaction and the ratio in which they react, for example $\mathrm{CaCO_{3} + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_{2} + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Knowing what gas or product a reaction makes is needed before choosing a sensible way to measure how much of it has formed.

prerequisites.statement: The gradient (steepness) of a line on a graph is found by dividing the change in the vertical value by the corresponding change in the horizontal value, between two points on the line.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Reading rate from a volume/mass-time graph is entirely a gradient calculation; without this skill the graphs in this lesson cannot be interpreted correctly.

prerequisites.statement: Dividing a quantity in one unit by a quantity in another unit (for example, $\mathrm{cm^3}$ by seconds) gives a new quantity with a combined unit, such as $\mathrm{cm^3/s}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A mean rate is always reported with a combined unit; without this, a correct numerical answer can still be marked wrong for a missing or invented unit.

diagnostic_items.question: A straight line on a graph passes through the points $(0,\ 0)$ and $(10,\ 30)$. Calculate the gradient of the line, showing the division you use.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Gradient $=\dfrac{\text{change in vertical value}}{\text{change in horizontal value}} = \dfrac{30-0}{10-0} = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3$.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has divided the horizontal change by the vertical change, the wrong way round; they know a division is needed but not which quantity goes on top.
The learner has read off the rise only and has not divided by the horizontal change at all, treating 'how much it went up' as the gradient.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks the prerequisite directly: a gradient is a vertical change divided by the matching horizontal change, not a single read-off. Every rate in this lesson is read from a graph in exactly this way.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner to mark the two points on the line, draw the right-angled triangle between them, label the vertical side 30 and the horizontal side 10, and then write the division vertical $\div$ horizontal before putting any numbers in.

diagnostic_items.question: A reaction produces $30\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of gas in $10\ \mathrm{s}$. The volume is divided by the time. State the value and the unit of the answer.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $30 \div 10 = 3$, and the unit is the first unit divided by the second, $\mathrm{cm^3/s}$ (read as 'centimetres cubed per second'), so the answer is $3\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has carried over only the unit of the quantity on top and has dropped the time, so the answer no longer says 'per second'.
The learner treats the unit as optional decoration rather than as part of the answer, which loses the mark even when the number is right.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks that dividing a quantity in one unit by a quantity in another produces a combined unit. A mean rate is always quoted with such a unit, so a correct number with a missing or invented unit is still marked wrong.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner to write the division with the units left in, $\dfrac{30\ \mathrm{cm^3}}{10\ \mathrm{s}}$, and to carry the units through the calculation exactly as the numbers are carried through, giving $3\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$.

theory_blocks.title: Rate is a speed, not a total
theory_blocks.body:
Two cars can arrive at the same destination, but one gets there in ten minutes and the other in an hour; both travel the same distance, but only one travels fast.

Reaction rate works the same way. Two experiments can both end up producing exactly the same total volume of gas, but one reaches that total in 30 seconds and the other takes five minutes;

asking 'which one finished with more gas?' tells you nothing about which reaction was faster.

Rate means [[blue:change per unit time]]: how much product appears, or how much reactant is used up, for each second that passes.

To measure it, you need two things: a quantity that changes as the reaction happens (gas volume, or the mass of the reaction flask as gas escapes), and the time over which you measure that change.

theory_blocks.title: Mean rate and the graph's gradient
theory_blocks.body:
For a gas-producing reaction, the **mean rate** over a time interval is defined as:
$$\text{mean rate} = \dfrac{\text{change in quantity measured}}{\text{time taken}}$$

If a gas syringe reads $30\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ after $10\ \mathrm{s}$, starting from $0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, the mean rate over that interval is $\dfrac{30}{10} = 3.0\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$.

The same calculation works for mass loss, in $\mathrm{g/s}$, when the reaction mixture is weighed on a balance as gas escapes instead.

On a volume-time or mass-time graph, this calculation is exactly the **gradient** of the line between two points: steeper means faster.

Because the gradient usually changes as the reaction proceeds (steep at the start, flatter later), a gradient calculated 'at a point' really means the gradient of a short interval or tangent around that point,

not the gradient of the whole curve from start to finish.

theory_blocks.title: Final volume and rate answer different questions
theory_blocks.body:
It is tempting to read 'how fast' straight off the height a graph eventually reaches, but height and steepness answer two separate questions.

The **final volume** (or final mass lost) depends on how much of the limiting reactant was present — [[blue:more marble chips, more gas can eventually be produced]], however fast or slowly the reaction runs.

The **rate** depends on the conditions (concentration, surface area, temperature, catalyst) and shows up as the steepness of the curve, especially near the start, before the reactants begin to run out and the curve flattens.

Two experiments using the same mass of the same solid, reacting with excess acid, will reach the same final volume regardless of whether the solid is a single lump or crushed into powder — the amount of gas that can ever be made is fixed by the amount of solid.

What differs between a lump and a powder is only how quickly that fixed final volume is reached, which is exactly what the figure below is built to show.
