assets.caption: Two experiments, same mass (0.20 g) of calcium carbonate reacting with excess dilute hydrochloric acid, so both approach the same final volume of $48\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$. Curve A (powdered chips) rises far more steeply at the start: its mean rate over the first 10 s is $1.7\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$, against $0.6\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$ for curve B (one large lump), even though both curves are heading for the same final height.
assets.purpose: Lets a learner read initial gradient and final value as two separate, independently verified facts from the same pair of curves, directly countering the final-height misconception.

theory_blocks.title: Five factors, one definition of catalyst
theory_blocks.body:
Five conditions change how fast a reaction goes: **concentration** of a dissolved reactant (more particles in the same volume), **pressure** of a reacting gas (more particles in the same volume, for gases), **surface area** of a solid reactant (more of it exposed where a liquid or gas can reach it), **temperature**, and the presence of a **catalyst**.

Increasing concentration, pressure, surface area or temperature all increase rate; a catalyst increases rate without being a reactant at all.

A **catalyst** is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up, and without appearing in the overall balanced equation as a reactant or product;

the same mass of catalyst is present, chemically unchanged, at the end of the reaction as at the start, and it can be recovered and reused.

theory_blocks.title: Building a fair test

keywords.definition: The change in a measured quantity (gas volume or mass) divided by the time taken for that change.
The steepness of a graph's line between two points; on a volume/mass-time graph, this is the rate at that interval.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being chemically used up or changed in mass.
An experiment in which only one independent variable is changed, with every other variable that could affect the result kept constant.
The single factor that is deliberately changed between trials in a fair test.
A factor, other than the independent variable, that is deliberately kept constant between trials so it cannot affect the comparison.

worked_examples.statement: **A first ten seconds.** In the first 10 s of a reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid, the reading on a gas syringe rises from $0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ to $30\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. Calculate the mean rate of gas production over this interval.
solution: Change in volume $= 30 - 0 = 30\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.
Time taken $= 10\ \mathrm{s}$.
Mean rate $= \dfrac{30}{10} = 3.0\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Checked by substitution: $3.0\ \mathrm{cm^3/s} \times 10\ \mathrm{s} = 30\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, matching the volume given.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading an interval, not the whole curve.** Using curve A from the figure above (powdered chips), the gas volume reads $28.5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ at $t=20\ \mathrm{s}$ and $40.1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ at $t=40\ \mathrm{s}$. Calculate the mean rate between $t=20\ \mathrm{s}$ and $t=40\ \mathrm{s}$, and explain why it is lower than the mean rate over the first 10 s.
solution: Change in volume $= 40.1 - 28.5 = 11.6\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.
Time taken $= 40-20 = 20\ \mathrm{s}$.
Mean rate $= \dfrac{11.6}{20} = 0.58\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$, noticeably lower than the $1.7\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$ measured over the first 10 s.

The rate falls because the reactants (acid and calcium carbonate) are being used up as the reaction proceeds, so fewer particles remain to collide and react each second; the curve flattens as it approaches its final volume.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the direct resolution of the declared gap between 'gradient at an interval' and 'final quantity': the same curve gives a different mean rate depending on which interval you pick, and both are legitimate answers to different questions.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the overall change from $t=0$ to $t=40$ (dividing the full $40.1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ by $40\ \mathrm{s}$) when asked for the rate over a specific later interval, rather than using only the volumes at the start and end of that interval.

worked_examples.statement: **Same ending, different story.** Using the figure above, a student says 'curve A and curve B end up almost level by $t=180\ \mathrm{s}$, around $48\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ and $44\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, so the two reactions were roughly equally fast.' Evaluate this claim.
solution: The student is comparing the two curves' heights near the end of the time shown, not their steepness, which answers a different question from 'how fast'.

Over the first 10 s, curve A rises to $17.4\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ (mean rate $1.7\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$) while curve B rises only to $6.3\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ (mean rate $0.6\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$): curve A is reacting roughly three times as fast at the start.

Both curves are heading towards the same final volume ($48\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, fixed by the same 0.20 g mass of calcium carbonate reacting with excess acid); curve B has simply not finished rising yet by $t=180\ \mathrm{s}$, while curve A has already levelled off.
The student's claim is incorrect: the two reactions were not equally fast, they are simply approaching the same final total, which is a property of the amount of solid used, not of the rate.
worked_examples.interpretation: This worked example targets the final-height misconception directly, using numbers taken from the same figure the learner has already studied.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Comparing the two curves only at the latest time shown, instead of comparing their gradients over the same early interval.

worked_examples.statement: **Designing a fair test.** A student wants to find out whether increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid increases the rate of its reaction with magnesium ribbon. Describe a fair test, stating the independent variable, the variables that must be controlled, and a suitable way to measure rate.
solution: Independent variable: concentration of hydrochloric acid, for example comparing $1.0\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ with $2.0\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$, using the same volume of acid (for example $50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$) each time.

Controlled variables: the length and mass of magnesium ribbon used, the volume of acid, the temperature of the acid, and the apparatus used to collect the gas, must all be identical between the two runs.

Dependent variable and method: measure the volume of hydrogen gas collected in a gas syringe at regular time intervals (for example every 10 s) for both concentrations, and compare the mean rate over the same early interval (or the initial gradient) for each.

Only the acid's concentration should differ between the two runs; if the mass of magnesium or the temperature were also allowed to differ, any difference in rate could not be attributed to concentration alone.
worked_examples.interpretation: Naming specific, checkable values (concentrations, volumes) rather than leaving the design vague is what an exam mark scheme rewards.

guided_exercises.statement: A conical flask containing magnesium ribbon and dilute hydrochloric acid is placed on a balance. The total mass is $150.0\ \mathrm{g}$ at the start, and $149.4\ \mathrm{g}$ after $40\ \mathrm{s}$, as hydrogen gas escapes. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over this interval, including units.
hints: Find the change in mass first: how much mass has been lost?
Mean rate is always a change divided by the time taken for that change.
The unit of a mass-loss rate combines a mass unit and a time unit, just as the gas-volume rate combined $\mathrm{cm^3}$ and $\mathrm{s}$.
common_errors: Dividing the final mass (149.4 g) by the time instead of the change in mass, giving a meaningless rate.

guided_exercises.statement: A student investigating the effect of temperature on rate reacts magnesium with $1.0\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ hydrochloric acid at $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, then repeats the experiment with $2.0\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ hydrochloric acid at $40\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The second run is much faster. Explain why this result cannot be used to conclude that raising the temperature increased the rate, and describe the one change needed to fix the test.
hints: List every variable that differs between the two runs, not just the one the student was interested in.
If two variables both changed and the result changed too, can you say which one caused it?
What would the second run need to keep the same as the first, so that only temperature differs?
guided_exercises.answer: Two variables changed between the two runs: both the temperature (20 to 40 °C) and the acid concentration (1.0 to 2.0 mol/dm³). Since either change alone could have increased the rate, the faster result cannot be attributed to temperature specifically — it might be mostly or entirely due to the higher concentration. To fix the test, the second run should use the same $1.0\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ acid concentration as the first, changing only the temperature to $40\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
common_errors: Accepting the result as evidence for temperature because temperature was the variable the student intended to test, without checking what else changed.

exercises.statement: Two experiments, X and Y, both produce a final volume of $60\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of gas. Experiment X reaches $50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ after only 20 s and levels off at $60\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ soon afterwards; experiment Y reaches just $15\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ after 20 s and is still rising slowly. A student claims 'X and Y must have reacted at the same rate, since they both end at 60 cm³.' Explain what is wrong with this claim.
exercises.answer: Reaching the same final volume only shows that both experiments had the same amount of limiting reactant available to produce gas; it says nothing about how fast each one reacted. Experiment X's steep early rise (50 cm³ in the first 20 s, a mean rate of $2.5\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$) shows it reacted far faster than experiment Y (15 cm³ in 20 s, a mean rate of $0.75\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$), even though both are heading for the same eventual total.

exercises.statement: Hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes very slowly on its own into water and oxygen gas. Adding a small amount of manganese(IV) oxide powder makes the decomposition much faster, and at the end of the reaction the same mass of manganese(IV) oxide can be recovered, filtered out and reused. Explain why manganese(IV) oxide is described as a catalyst rather than as a reactant in this reaction.
exercises.answer: A reactant is used up as a reaction proceeds, so its mass decreases. Manganese(IV) oxide is recovered at the end with exactly the same mass as was added, showing it has not been chemically used up; it has only provided a faster pathway for hydrogen peroxide to decompose. Because it increases the rate without being consumed, and does not appear as a product, it is a catalyst, not a reactant.
common_errors: Assuming anything added to speed up a reaction must be 'partly used up', without checking the evidence (its mass is unchanged) that actually settles the question.

exercises.statement: A student wants to test whether crushing marble chips into powder increases the rate of reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid, compared with using the same mass of chips uncrushed. State the independent variable, name two variables that must be controlled, and suggest a suitable dependent variable to measure.
exercises.answer: Independent variable: the form of the calcium carbonate (powder versus uncrushed chips), with the same total mass used in each case. Controlled variables (any two): the mass of calcium carbonate used, the volume and concentration of the acid, and the temperature. Dependent variable: the volume of carbon dioxide gas collected in a gas syringe at regular time intervals, used to compare the gradient of each volume-time graph.

exercises.statement: A cook notices that a stew cooks faster when the vegetables are chopped into small pieces than when they are left whole, and faster still at a rolling boil than at a gentle simmer. Using the ideas from this lesson, identify which rate factor each observation corresponds to, and explain, in terms of a measurable rate (not just 'faster'), how you could compare the two chopping methods fairly.
exercises.answer: Chopping vegetables into smaller pieces increases their exposed surface area, which is the same factor that makes powdered calcium carbonate react faster than a single lump. Boiling harder raises the cooking liquid's temperature, which is the temperature factor. To compare the chopping methods fairly, a single measurable change would need to be tracked over time (for example, how much the vegetable pieces' mass decreases as they soften and release liquid, or a texture/firmness reading at fixed time intervals) with every other variable — same vegetable, same total starting mass, same liquid, same temperature — kept identical between the whole-piece and chopped trials, changing only the surface area.

exercises.statement: Define the key terms used in the study of 'Measuring rate and testing factors'.
exercises.answer: Key definitions should cover the main concepts from 'Measuring rate and testing factors' using precise scientific language.

exercises.statement: Explain one key concept from 'Measuring rate and testing factors' and give a real-world example.
exercises.answer: A full answer should clearly explain the concept using correct terminology and link it to a practical everyday example.

exam_questions.statement: A gas syringe is used to collect the hydrogen produced when magnesium reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The table shows the volume collected at six times. Time / s: 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90. Volume / cm$^3$: 0.0, 27.1, 41.9, 50.1, 54.6, 58.4. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 15 s, calculate the mean rate between 45 s and 90 s, and explain why these two mean rates are different.
exam_questions.answer: Mean rate over the first 15 s $= \dfrac{27.1 - 0.0}{15} = 1.8\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$ (to 2 s.f.). Mean rate between 45 s and 90 s $= \dfrac{58.4 - 50.1}{90-45} = \dfrac{8.3}{45} = 0.18\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$ (to 2 s.f.). The rate is much lower later in the reaction because the reactants are being used up: as magnesium and acid particles become less concentrated/less available, there are fewer successful collisions each second, so the volume of gas produced per second falls, which is seen on the graph as a flattening curve.
mark_scheme: Calculates change in volume for 0-15 s as 27.1 cm³.
Divides by the correct time (15 s) to give 1.8 cm³/s.
Calculates change in volume for 45-90 s as 8.3 cm³, divided by 45 s, to give 0.18 cm³/s.
States that the rate decreases as the reaction proceeds.
Explains the decrease in terms of reactants being used up / fewer particles available to collide and react.

exam_questions.statement: A student investigating the effect of surface area on rate reacts 1.0 g of calcium carbonate powder with 50 cm$^3$ of 1.0 mol/dm$^3$ hydrochloric acid at 20 °C, then separately reacts 1.0 g of calcium carbonate marble chips with 50 cm$^3$ of 2.0 mol/dm$^3$ hydrochloric acid, also at 20 °C. The powder reaction is faster. Evaluate whether this comparison is a fair test of the effect of surface area, and state what should be changed.
exam_questions.answer: This is not a fair test, because two variables differ between the runs: the form of the calcium carbonate (powder versus chips, the intended surface-area variable) and the concentration of the acid (1.0 versus 2.0 mol/dm³, which was not supposed to change). Since a higher acid concentration would also increase rate on its own, the faster result for the powder cannot be attributed to surface area alone. The acid concentration should be kept the same (for example, both at 1.0 mol/dm³) in both runs, changing only the form of the calcium carbonate.
mark_scheme: States that the test is not fair.
Identifies that both the form of the solid and the acid concentration differ between the two runs.
Explains that the faster result cannot be attributed to surface area alone because concentration also changed.
States the correction: use the same acid concentration in both runs.

challenge_questions.statement: In a new experiment, excess dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a sample of calcium carbonate chips, and the reaction is left to go to completion. The final volume of carbon dioxide collected is $72\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, measured at room temperature and pressure, where 1 mole of any gas occupies $24\,000\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate (molar mass $100\ \mathrm{g/mol}$) used, and explain why this calculation does not need any information about the rate of the reaction.
hints: Start from the final volume of gas and work out how many moles of $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ that represents.
Use the balanced equation $\mathrm{CaCO_{3} + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_{2} + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}$ to relate moles of $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ to moles of $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}$.
Think about what determines a reaction's final amount of product, as distinct from what determines how quickly it gets there.
challenge_questions.answer: Moles of $\mathrm{CO_{2}} = \dfrac{72}{24\,000} = 0.0030\ \mathrm{mol}$. Since $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}$ and $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ react/form in a 1:1 ratio, moles of $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} = 0.0030\ \mathrm{mol}$. Mass of $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} = 0.0030 \times 100 = 0.30\ \mathrm{g}$. This calculation uses only the final volume and the reacting ratio, neither of which depends on how fast the reaction happened; the final amount of product is fixed by the amount of limiting reactant (here, the calcium carbonate, since the acid is in excess), regardless of whether the reaction took 30 seconds or 30 minutes to finish.
common_errors: Trying to use a time value in the calculation, when the question provides only a final volume and asks for a quantity (mass) that depends on stoichiometry, not on rate.

challenge_questions.statement:
Marble chips (CaCO₃) react with dilute hydrochloric acid. A student measures the volume of CO₂ gas produced every 30 seconds.
(a) Sketch the graph of volume of CO₂ (y-axis) against time (x-axis). Label the line. (2 marks)
(b) On the same axes, sketch and label the line you would expect if: (i) the acid were more concentrated, (ii) the marble chips were ground to a powder. (2 marks)
(c) Explain, using collision theory, why increasing concentration increases the rate. (3 marks)
(d) Explain why all three lines reach the same final volume. (1 mark)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) A curve that rises steeply at first then levels off to a plateau (horizontal line).
(b) (i) Steeper initial gradient, reaches the same final volume sooner. (ii) Also steeper — reaches the same final volume even more quickly.
(c) Higher concentration means more acid particles per unit volume. This increases the frequency of collisions between acid particles and marble chip particles per second. More frequent collisions mean more successful collisions per second, so the rate of reaction increases.
(d) The same total amount of marble and acid are used in each experiment, so the same total amount of CO₂ is produced. Only the speed of production changes, not the total amount.

mcq.stem: Two reactions, P and Q, both eventually produce 40 cm³ of gas. Reaction P reaches 35 cm³ within the first 10 s; reaction Q reaches only 8 cm³ in the first 10 s but keeps rising for several more minutes. Which reaction was faster, and why?

options.text: Reaction Q, because it keeps producing gas for longer overall.
options.why_wrong: reacting for longer overall is a consequence of being slower, not evidence of being faster; rate is about steepness, not duration.

options.text: Reaction P, because its early gradient (volume produced per second) is much steeper.
Neither; both are equally fast, since they reach the same final volume.
options.why_wrong: reaching the same final volume reflects the same amount of limiting reactant, not the same rate.

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the exact final time for each reaction.
options.why_wrong: the early gradient, already given, is sufficient to compare rate; the final time is not needed.

mcq.explanation: Rate is read from the steepness (gradient) of the graph; reaction P's much steeper rise in the first 10 s shows it reacted faster, regardless of the fact both reactions reach the same eventual total.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly describes a catalyst?

options.text: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction but is slowly used up, more slowly than the main reactants.
options.why_wrong: a catalyst is not used up at all, however slowly; its mass is unchanged at the end of the reaction.

options.text: A substance that must be present in large amounts to have any effect on rate.
options.why_wrong: catalysts are typically effective in small amounts and do not need to be present in a large quantity.

options.text: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is chemically unchanged and present in the same mass at the end of the reaction.
A substance that changes the products formed by a reaction.
options.why_wrong: a catalyst changes how fast the reaction reaches its products, not which products are formed.

mcq.explanation: By definition, a catalyst speeds up a reaction without being chemically changed or used up; its mass is the same at the start and end of the reaction.

mcq.stem: A student tests the effect of acid concentration on rate by reacting magnesium with 1.0 mol/dm³ acid at 20 °C, then with 2.0 mol/dm³ acid at 30 °C. Why is this not a fair test?

options.text: Because concentration should never be tested using a gas syringe.
options.why_wrong: a gas syringe is a perfectly suitable way to measure rate when testing concentration; this is not the problem with the test.

options.text: Because magnesium is not an appropriate reactant for investigating concentration.
options.why_wrong: magnesium reacting with acid is a standard, appropriate reaction for investigating rate factors; this is not the issue.

options.text: Because only one trial was carried out at each concentration.
options.why_wrong: repeating trials improves reliability, but it is not what makes this specific test unfair; the real problem is that two variables changed at once.

options.text: Because both concentration and temperature were changed between the two runs, so any difference in rate cannot be attributed to concentration alone.

mcq.explanation: A fair test changes only the independent variable; here, temperature changed alongside concentration, so the result cannot be attributed to concentration alone.

mcq.stem: A reaction produces 24 cm³ of gas in the first 8 s. What is the mean rate of reaction over this interval?

options.text: 3.0 cm³/s
0.33 cm³/s
options.why_wrong: this comes from dividing 8 by 24 instead of 24 by 8, inverting the calculation.

options.text: 16 cm³/s
options.why_wrong: this comes from subtracting 8 from 24 instead of dividing; rate is a quotient, not a difference.

options.text: 32 cm³/s
options.why_wrong: this comes from adding 24 and 8 instead of dividing; mean rate is volume divided by time, not their sum.

flashcards.front: How is the mean rate of a reaction calculated from a gas-volume or mass measurement?
flashcards.back: Mean rate = (change in quantity measured) / (time taken), for example cm³/s or g/s.

flashcards.front: What is a catalyst?
flashcards.back: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being chemically used up; its mass is unchanged at the end of the reaction.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between the final volume reached on a gas-volume-time graph and its gradient?
flashcards.back: The final volume depends on the amount of limiting reactant used; the gradient (steepness) at a point shows the rate at that time. A faster reaction and a slower one can reach the same final volume.

flashcards.front: Curve X ends higher than curve Y on a volume-time graph. Does this mean reaction X was faster?
flashcards.back: Not necessarily. The final height reflects the amount of product that could ever form, not how quickly it formed; rate must be judged from the gradient (steepness), not the final height.

flashcards.front: A student changes both acid concentration and temperature between two trials testing 'the effect of concentration'. Why is this test not fair?
flashcards.back: Because two variables changed at once, any difference in rate could be due to either one; a fair test changes only the independent variable being investigated, keeping everything else constant.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Whichever graph reaches the highest final value (the largest total volume of gas or mass lost) shows the fastest reaction.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners read a graph the way they would read a race result, looking at where the lines end up rather than how quickly they got there, especially when both curves are shown ending at different times.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner points to the curve with the greater final height, even when that curve was still rising slowly at every early time shown, and calls it 'faster'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Rate is about steepness (how much changes per second), not about the final total; a reaction's final amount of product depends on how much limiting reactant was used, which can be the same in two experiments that react at very different speeds.
misconceptions.remediation: Show two graphs with the same final volume but very different early gradients, cover the ends of both curves, and ask only 'which curve is steeper in the first 10 seconds?' before asking which reaction 'finished higher'.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A catalyst is a kind of reactant: it gets used up during the reaction, just more slowly or in a smaller amount than the other reactants.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Catalysts are added to a reaction mixture in the same way reactants are, so learners group them with reactants and assume anything added must be consumed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that a catalyst's mass will have decreased by the end of the reaction, or that a reaction would eventually 'run out' of catalyst the way it runs out of a reactant.
misconceptions.correct_model: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by providing an easier pathway for it, but is chemically unchanged and present in exactly the same mass at the end of the reaction as at the start; it is not written into the overall reactants in a symbol equation.
misconceptions.remediation: Weigh a catalyst (such as manganese(IV) oxide used with hydrogen peroxide) before and after it has catalysed a reaction to completion, and show the mass is unchanged, while a true reactant used in the same reaction has clearly decreased or disappeared.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: If you want to know whether a factor (such as temperature) affects rate, you can still draw a valid conclusion even if you also changed a second factor (such as concentration) between the two test runs, as long as you changed temperature 'the most'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners under time pressure in practical work often change more than one variable to 'make the effect bigger and easier to see', without realising this removes their ability to say which change caused the result.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner designs or accepts an experiment where two variables differ between the test and the control, then attributes the whole observed difference in rate to only one of them.
misconceptions.correct_model: A fair test changes only one independent variable at a time and holds every other variable that could affect the result constant; if two variables change together, any difference in rate cannot be attributed to either one alone.
misconceptions.remediation: Present a flawed experiment where both acid concentration and temperature were changed between two trials, and ask what, specifically, cannot be concluded from the result, before redesigning it as a fair test.

common_mistakes.mistake: Judging which of two reactions was faster from the final height reached on a volume-time or mass-time graph.
common_mistakes.why: A graph's end point is the most visually obvious feature, especially when curves are compared side by side.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always compare the gradient (steepness) over the same early time interval on both curves, ignoring where each curve ends up.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a catalyst is slowly consumed, like a reactant used in a smaller amount.
common_mistakes.why: A catalyst is physically added to the reaction mixture, which makes it easy to group mentally with the true reactants.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember the defining test: a catalyst's mass is unchanged at the end of the reaction; if mass has decreased, it was a reactant, not a catalyst.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing two variables at once when designing or evaluating a 'fair test' of one rate factor.
common_mistakes.why: Changing more than one variable can make an effect look bigger and easier to see, which feels like good experimental design under time pressure.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before accepting a result, list every variable that differs between the two runs being compared; if more than one does, the result cannot be attributed to any single factor.

exam_notes: Always state the unit of a mean rate explicitly (cm³/s, g/s); an otherwise correct numerical answer without a unit, or with an invented one, loses marks.
When asked to compare two experiments' rates from a graph, quote the gradient (or a mean rate calculated over a matching interval) for each, rather than only describing the curves in words.

When evaluating or designing a fair test, name the independent variable, at least two controlled variables, and the dependent variable (the measured signal) explicitly; 'keep everything else the same' without naming anything rarely earns full marks.

summary.big_idea: Rate is a gradient (change per second), read from the steepness of a graph over a chosen interval, and is a completely different quantity from the final amount of product a reaction reaches.
key_points: Mean rate = change in quantity measured / time taken, with a combined unit such as cm³/s or g/s.
On a volume/mass-time graph, rate at a point is the gradient there, not the final height the curve reaches.
Concentration, pressure, surface area and temperature all increase rate when increased; a catalyst increases rate without being used up.
A fair test changes exactly one independent variable, keeping every other variable that could affect rate constant.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Rate is steepness, not final height: two curves can finish at the same volume while one reacted far faster than the other.

exit_check.question: Curve M reaches 50 cm³ in 15 s and levels off there. Curve N also reaches 50 cm³, but only after 90 s. Which reaction was faster, and what single piece of evidence from the curves justifies your answer?
exit_check.answer: Curve M was faster. Both curves reach the same final volume (50 cm³), showing they used the same amount of limiting reactant, but curve M's much steeper early gradient (reaching 50 cm³ in only 15 s, against 90 s for curve N) shows it produced gas far more quickly.

03_Collision_theory_explains_rate.json.title: Collision theory explains rate
03_Collision_theory_explains_rate.json.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Explain, in terms of particle collisions, why not every collision between reacting particles results in a reaction, and define a successful (effective) collision using activation energy.

Explain how concentration, pressure and surface area change the frequency of particle collisions, and how temperature changes both collision frequency and the proportion of particles with enough energy to react.

Explain how a catalyst increases rate by providing a reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, without being used up, without changing the products, and without altering the overall energy change of the reaction.

prerequisites.statement: A reaction's rate can be measured from a volume/mass-time graph as a gradient, and concentration, surface area, temperature and catalysts are known (from measurement) to change rate.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson explains the causes behind the factors already measured and observed in the previous lesson; the factors are not new, only the mechanism behind them is.

prerequisites.statement: Even a reaction that releases energy overall (exothermic) must get over an energy barrier, the activation energy, before reactant bonds can break and product bonds can form.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A successful collision is defined entirely in terms of this energy barrier; without it, 'enough energy to react' has no fixed meaning.

prerequisites.statement: Particles in a gas or in solution are in constant, random motion, and at any instant not all particles in a sample are moving at the same speed or have the same kinetic energy.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Explaining the temperature effect correctly depends on there being a spread of particle energies, some above and some below the activation energy, rather than every particle having the same energy.

diagnostic_items.question: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gives out a great deal of energy when it reacts, yet the mixture can sit in a sealed tube for hours without reacting until a spark is applied. What does this show about the energy needed before a reaction can begin?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Even a reaction that releases energy overall has an energy barrier to get over first: the colliding particles must have at least a certain minimum energy, the **activation energy**, before reactant bonds can start to break. The spark supplies that starting energy; without it, almost no collision is energetic enough, so the mixture appears unreactive.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The reaction must take in energy overall, otherwise it would start on its own.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is confusing the energy barrier at the start with the overall energy change, and so assumes anything needing a spark must be endothermic.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The particles are not touching, so the spark pushes them together.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner thinks collisions are the only requirement and treats the spark as a way of causing contact, rather than as a way of supplying energy to particles that are already colliding constantly.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks the prerequisite that there is an energy barrier before any reaction, independent of whether the reaction is exothermic. A successful collision is defined entirely in terms of that barrier, so without it the phrase 'enough energy to react' has no fixed meaning.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch an energy profile for an exothermic reaction with the learner: mark the reactant level, the peak and the lower product level, and have them point to the hump (the activation energy) and separately to the overall drop, naming each one before moving on.

diagnostic_items.question: Do all the particles in a sample of gas at 20 °C have the same kinetic energy? Explain your answer.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. The particles move randomly and collide constantly, so at any instant they are moving at a wide range of speeds and therefore have a range of kinetic energies. The temperature tells you the *average* kinetic energy: some particles have much more than that average and some much less.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, because they are all at the same temperature.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is treating temperature as a property each individual particle carries, rather than as a measure of the average energy of a whole sample with a spread of energies.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, because they are all the same kind of particle with the same mass.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner assumes identical particles must be moving identically, and has not pictured the random collisions that continually redistribute energy between them.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks the prerequisite that there is a spread of particle energies. The explanation of why a small temperature rise causes a large rate increase depends on some particles lying above the activation energy and most lying below it; if every particle had the same energy, that explanation collapses.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner to picture a hundred particles in a box after a few seconds of random collisions and to say whether every one is moving at exactly the same speed; then introduce 'average' as the word temperature actually reports, and ask which particles are the ones able to react.

theory_blocks.title: Most collisions fail
theory_blocks.body:
In a test tube of reacting solution, billions of particle collisions happen every second, yet many reactions still take minutes to finish.

If every collision caused a reaction, almost everything would react in an instant. The only way to explain a measurable, finite rate is that most collisions do not lead to a reaction at all — the particles simply touch and bounce apart,

completely unchanged, like two people brushing past each other in a crowded corridor.

What makes the difference between a collision that fails and one that succeeds? It is not how hard the particles hit, in some vague sense, but whether the particles involved have, between them, enough kinetic energy to start breaking the bonds that hold the reactants together.

Only collisions that clear this energy threshold go on to become a reaction; this threshold has a name — [[blue:activation energy]] — and it is central to everything else in this lesson.

theory_blocks.title: Defining a successful collision
theory_blocks.body:
The **activation energy**, $E_a$, is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have, combined, for a collision to be able to start breaking reactant bonds and lead to a reaction.

A **successful (effective) collision** is one in which the colliding particles meet this condition; an **unsuccessful collision** is one that does not, however frequent collisions are overall.

Reaction rate therefore depends on two separate things, multiplied together in effect: how often particles collide (**collision frequency**) and what fraction of those collisions have enough energy to succeed (set by $E_a$ and by how much kinetic energy the particles have).

Changing a condition can increase rate by raising either of these — or, for a catalyst, by lowering the energy bar that collisions need to clear in the first place.

theory_blocks.title: Concentration, pressure and surface area: more chances to meet
theory_blocks.body:
Concentration, pressure (for a gas) and surface area (for a solid) all increase rate by the same underlying mechanism: increasing **collision frequency**, without changing $E_a$ or the particles' average energy.

A more concentrated solution packs more dissolved particles into the same volume, so a given particle is statistically more likely to meet a reacting partner in a given second.

A higher gas pressure packs more gas particles into the same volume, for the same reason. A solid broken into smaller pieces exposes more of its particles directly to a surrounding liquid or gas,

so more collisions with the solid's surface can happen each second, even though the total amount of solid has not changed.

Because $E_a$ and the particles' typical energy are unaffected by any of these three factors, the *fraction* of collisions that succeed stays the same; rate increases purely because there are more collisions overall for that same fraction to act on.

assets.caption: Same total amount of solid (16 unit squares) in both panels. Crushing it into four separate pieces doubles the exposed edge where acid particles (red circles) can reach and collide with it, from 16 units to 32 units, without changing $E_a$ or the particles' energy — only the collision frequency rises.
assets.purpose: Makes the collision-frequency mechanism for surface area visible and quantitatively honest: same total solid, counted exposed boundary, verified by direct count before drawing.

theory_blocks.title: Temperature changes energy, not amount
theory_blocks.body:
Temperature is the one factor that works mainly through the *energy* route rather than the frequency route. Heating a sample does not add particles — the number of moles of reactant present is exactly what it was before heating.

What changes is that the same particles now move faster and carry more kinetic energy on average, so a larger proportion of all collisions now have, between the colliding particles, at least $E_a$ of energy.

Because the number of particles with very high energy is small and grows steeply with temperature, [[blue:even a modest temperature rise (for example 10 °C) can roughly double the proportion of collisions that succeed]], which is why reaction rates are often strikingly sensitive to temperature.

Collision frequency also rises a little, because faster particles travel further each second and so meet more partners, but this frequency effect alone is far too small to explain the size of the rate increases actually observed;

the energy effect dominates.

theory_blocks.title: A catalyst lowers the bar, not the drop
theory_blocks.body:
A **catalyst** provides an alternative route from reactants to products with a lower activation energy than the uncatalysed route.

Because more of the colliding particles now have at least this lower activation energy, a larger fraction of collisions becomes successful at the same temperature,

so the reaction speeds up — without needing any extra heating, and without the catalyst itself being used up.

The energy profile diagram below makes the distinction precise: both the catalysed and uncatalysed curves start at the same reactants' energy and end at the same products' energy, so the overall energy change, $\Delta H$, is identical either way;

only the height of the hump in between — the activation energy that has to be climbed — is lower for the catalysed path. A catalyst changes the route, not the destination.

assets.caption: Energy profile for the same exothermic reaction, uncatalysed (red, $E_\mathrm{a}=80\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) and catalysed (navy, dashed, $E_\mathrm{a}=50\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$). Each double-headed arrow runs from the reactants' energy level up to the peak of its own curve. Both paths start and finish at the same levels, so the overall energy change is the same, $\Delta H=-40\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ (green arrow on the right); only the height of the hump is lower for the catalysed path.
assets.purpose: Shows both activation energies measured correctly from the reactant level to the peak of the corresponding curve, with labels clear of both curves, and marks the overall energy change so that students can see the catalyst changes only the barrier.

keywords.definition: The model that a reaction occurs only when particles collide with at least the activation energy, explaining how each rate factor acts.
The minimum combined energy that colliding particles need for a collision to lead to a reaction, usually given the symbol Ea.
A collision between reacting particles that meets or exceeds the activation energy and so leads to a reaction.
How often particles collide with each other per unit time; increased by higher concentration, pressure or surface area.
A substance that increases rate by providing a reaction pathway with lower activation energy, without being used up or changing the products.
A diagram plotting energy against reaction progress, showing the reactants' and products' energy and the activation-energy barrier between them.

worked_examples.statement: **A collision that fails.** Two reacting particles collide directly, yet no new substance appears and both particles move apart completely unchanged. Using collision theory, explain how this result is possible.
solution: A collision alone is not enough to cause a reaction; the particles must also have, between them, at least the activation energy, $E_a$, needed to begin breaking bonds.
If the colliding particles' combined kinetic energy was below $E_a$, the collision was unsuccessful: the particles touch and separate again with no bonds broken and no new substance formed.
This is the normal outcome for the great majority of collisions in any reacting mixture, which is why reactions proceed at a finite, measurable rate rather than instantly.
worked_examples.interpretation: This directly pre-empts the 'any collision is enough' misconception by giving a concrete case where a real collision still fails.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining surface area, causally.** Using the figure of a single lump versus the same solid crushed into four pieces, explain in two linked steps why crushing the solid increases the rate of its reaction with acid.
solution: Step 1 (frequency): crushing the solid exposes far more of its particles directly to the surrounding acid — the exposed edge doubles from 16 to 32 units for the same total amount of solid — so many more solid-acid collisions can happen every second than when the same particles were hidden inside one compact lump.

Step 2 (rate): because $E_a$ and the particles' typical energy are unchanged, the same fraction of these collisions is successful as before; with more collisions happening per second, more successful collisions happen per second too, so the reaction proceeds noticeably faster, even though the total amount of solid, and so the final volume of gas, is unchanged.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Stopping at 'more surface area means more collisions' without the second step linking that to a faster rate because the success fraction itself has not changed.

worked_examples.statement: **Diagnosing a factor from a graph.** A chemist doubles the concentration of hydrochloric acid used in a marble-chip reaction and repeats the gas-collection experiment, keeping the mass of marble chips and every other condition the same. The new graph reaches the same final volume as before, but reaches it in about half the time, with a steeper early gradient. Identify which rate factor is responsible, and explain why the final volume is unaffected even though the rate has clearly increased.
solution: The factor responsible is concentration: doubling the acid's concentration packs more hydrochloric acid particles into the same volume, increasing how often acid particles collide with the marble chips' surface each second.

Because $E_a$ and the particles' energy are not affected by concentration, the same fraction of these collisions is successful; more collisions per second at the same success fraction means more product forms per second, which is seen as a steeper gradient and a shorter time to reach completion.

The final volume is set by the fixed mass of marble chips (the limiting reactant), not by concentration; since that mass has not changed, the same total amount of gas can ever be produced, however much faster it is now produced.
worked_examples.interpretation: This reasoning example deliberately reconnects to the rate-versus-final-volume distinction from the previous lesson, now explained causally rather than just observed.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding that a bigger final volume should also be expected, by assuming any factor that speeds up a reaction must also increase how much product it can make.

worked_examples.statement: **Catalytic converters.** Car exhaust gases pass over a catalyst (platinum and palladium) in a catalytic converter, which speeds up the conversion of polluting gases into less harmful ones, at exhaust-pipe temperatures that would otherwise react far too slowly to be useful. Explain, using the idea of activation energy, why fitting a catalyst is a more practical solution than simply running the car engine hotter to speed up the same reaction.
solution: The catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so a much larger fraction of collisions between the polluting gas particles already succeed at normal exhaust temperatures, without needing extra heat.

Raising the temperature instead would also increase the proportion of successful collisions, by giving particles more energy, but would require continuously supplying extra energy (worse fuel efficiency) and would push other engine temperatures to levels that risk damaging materials and increasing different pollutants (such as nitrogen oxides, which form faster at higher combustion temperatures).

Because the catalyst's own mass and chemical identity are unaffected by use, it keeps working for a long time (years of driving) at ordinary exhaust temperatures, making it a practical, reusable solution rather than a running energy cost.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.

guided_exercises.statement: A fixed 0.10 mol sample of a reacting gas mixture is heated from 20 °C to 40 °C in a sealed container. Explain, step by step, why the rate of the reaction increases, making clear what has and has not changed about the gas particles present.
hints: Start by stating exactly what has NOT changed: how many moles of gas are present before and after heating.
Now state what HAS changed about the particles themselves as a result of heating.
Finally, connect that change to the proportion of collisions that now have enough energy to succeed.
guided_exercises.answer: The amount of gas present is unchanged: 0.10 mol before heating and 0.10 mol after, so 'more particles' cannot be the explanation. What changes is that the same particles now have more kinetic energy on average and move faster. They collide a little more often, but, more importantly, a larger proportion of collisions now have combined energy at least equal to the activation energy, $E_a$. So there are more successful collisions each second, which is why the rate increases even though the number of particles present has stayed exactly the same.
common_errors: Explaining the increase by saying temperature 'creates more particles' or 'adds more reactant', rather than giving the same fixed particles more energy.

guided_exercises.statement: In an experiment, a reaction's rate noticeably increases between one run and the next, but a thermometer in the reaction mixture reads exactly the same temperature throughout both runs, and the same masses and concentrations of every reactant are used both times. Suggest what single change could explain the increased rate, and explain your reasoning.
hints: Temperature, concentration and the amount of each reactant have all been ruled out by the question; which other factor from this unit is left?
Think about what else could increase the fraction of successful collisions, or the collision frequency, without changing any of the ruled-out variables.
A catalyst does not need to be a 'reactant' in the usual sense, and does not show up in the masses or concentrations of the named reactants.
guided_exercises.answer: A catalyst was most likely added (or a more effective catalyst was used) in the second run. A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the reaction, increasing the fraction of collisions that succeed at the same temperature; because a catalyst is not one of the named reactants and is not used up, it would not show up as a change in the reactants' masses or concentrations, exactly matching the clues given.
common_errors: Assuming temperature must be responsible by default, without noticing the question has explicitly ruled it out.

exercises.statement: A student claims: 'Adding a catalyst to a reaction changes the products you get, which is how it helps the reaction along.' Evaluate this claim and give the correct explanation of how a catalyst actually helps a reaction along.
exercises.answer: The claim is incorrect. A catalyst does not change the identity of the products, or the overall energy change, $\Delta H$, of the reaction; the same products form whether or not a catalyst is used. What the catalyst actually does is provide an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of particle collisions have enough energy to succeed, making the same reaction, with the same products, happen faster.

exercises.statement: Explain why increasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction increases its rate, and explain why this particular factor would have no meaningful effect on a reaction taking place entirely between dissolved particles in a solution at atmospheric pressure.
exercises.answer: Increasing the pressure of a gas squeezes the same number of gas particles into a smaller volume, increasing how many gas particles are present in a given volume and so how often they collide with each other; this is the same collision-frequency mechanism as concentration, applied to gases. For a reaction between dissolved particles in solution, the particles are already essentially incompressible (a liquid's volume does not meaningfully shrink under ordinary pressure changes), so changing the external pressure does not pack the dissolved particles any closer together and has no meaningful effect on their collision frequency.

exercises.statement: A student says: 'A gas jar of hydrogen and oxygen gas can sit on a shelf for years without reacting, even though the particles inside it must be colliding constantly.' Use collision theory to explain why this observation does not contradict the idea that particles are always moving and colliding.
exercises.answer: The particles are indeed colliding extremely frequently, exactly as the student says; the observation is explained not by a lack of collisions but by the activation energy for this particular reaction being high, and room temperature providing too little energy for more than a vanishingly small fraction of collisions to succeed. Essentially none of the vast number of collisions happening every second have enough combined energy to break the strong bonds in $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{O_{2}}$, so no detectable reaction occurs, even over years, until something (such as a spark) supplies enough energy to a few particles to begin the reaction.
common_errors: Concluding that 'no reaction is happening' must mean 'no collisions are happening', rather than 'collisions are happening but essentially none of them are successful'.

exercises.statement: Food that is refrigerated spoils much more slowly than food left at room temperature, because the chemical reactions that cause spoilage proceed more slowly when cold. Using collision theory, explain why refrigeration slows these reactions, and explain why freezing food (well below 0 °C) slows spoilage even further than simple refrigeration.
exercises.answer: Refrigeration lowers the temperature of the food, which lowers the average kinetic energy of the particles involved in the spoilage reactions; this reduces the proportion of collisions with enough combined energy to exceed the activation energy for those reactions, so fewer collisions succeed each second and spoilage proceeds more slowly. Freezing lowers the temperature even further, reducing the successful-collision fraction still more; in addition, freezing solidifies the water in the food, which drastically restricts how often the dissolved particles involved in spoilage reactions can even meet and collide in the first place, combining a much lower success fraction with a much lower collision frequency.

exercises.statement: Define the key terms used in the study of 'Collision theory explains rate'.
exercises.answer: Key definitions should cover the main concepts from 'Collision theory explains rate' using precise scientific language.

exercises.statement: Explain one key concept from 'Collision theory explains rate' and give a real-world example.
exercises.answer: A full answer should clearly explain the concept using correct terminology and link it to a practical everyday example.

exam_questions.statement: Marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid. A student repeats the experiment using the same mass of marble, crushed into much smaller chips. Explain, in terms of collision frequency, why the reaction with smaller chips is faster, and state what happens to the total volume of gas eventually collected.
exam_questions.answer: Crushing the marble into smaller chips exposes much more of its surface to the surrounding acid, for the same total mass of marble; this means more marble particles are available at the surface to be struck by acid particles each second, so the frequency of successful collisions between the acid and the marble increases, which is seen as a faster rate (a steeper gas-volume-time graph). The total volume of gas eventually collected stays the same as before, because it is fixed by the mass of marble (the limiting reactant) present, which has not changed by crushing it.
mark_scheme: States that crushing exposes more surface area for the same mass of marble.
Links this to more frequent collisions between acid and marble particles.
Concludes correctly that this gives a faster rate / steeper graph.
States that the total (final) volume of gas is unchanged because the mass of marble is unchanged.

exam_questions.statement: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes very slowly at room temperature. Adding manganese(IV) oxide greatly increases the rate of decomposition. Using the idea of activation energy, explain how the catalyst achieves this, and state two things that remain unchanged about the reaction when the catalyst is used.
exam_questions.answer: Manganese(IV) oxide provides an alternative reaction pathway for the decomposition with a lower activation energy than the uncatalysed route; because collisions now need less combined energy to succeed, a much larger fraction of collisions between hydrogen peroxide particles are successful at room temperature, so the rate of decomposition increases sharply. Two things that remain unchanged: the products formed (water and oxygen gas, the same as without the catalyst) and the overall energy change, $\Delta H$, of the reaction (the catalyst changes only the height of the activation-energy barrier, not the energy difference between reactants and products).
mark_scheme: States that the catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy.
Links this to a larger fraction of collisions succeeding at the same temperature.
Concludes that this gives a faster rate of decomposition.

Correctly names one unchanged quantity: the products formed (water and oxygen) / the overall energy change ($\Delta H$) / the total volume of oxygen produced / the mass (and chemical identity) of the catalyst.
Correctly names a second, different unchanged quantity from this list.

challenge_questions.statement: A student proposes: 'Doubling the temperature (in °C) should roughly double the frequency of particle collisions, and that is the main reason a hotter reaction mixture reacts faster.' Explain what is wrong with this proposal, and state what the dominant cause of the rate increase actually is.
hints: Collision frequency depends on how fast particles move; does doubling a Celsius temperature double particle speed in the same simple way?
Separate the two effects of heating: what happens to collision frequency, and what happens to the fraction of collisions with enough energy to succeed.
Compare the sizes of these two effects: which one is big enough to explain the large rate increases often seen from a modest temperature rise?
challenge_questions.answer: The proposal is flawed for two reasons. First, 'doubling the temperature in °C' is not even a meaningful physical statement about particle energy, since particle kinetic energy relates to absolute temperature and to the spread of particle speeds, not to a simple doubling of a Celsius reading. Second, and more importantly, collision frequency only rises modestly with temperature (faster-moving particles meet slightly more often), far too little on its own to explain the often dramatic rate increases seen from a rise of only 10 °C. The dominant cause is instead the sharp increase in the proportion of particles whose energy exceeds the activation energy: because particle energies are spread over a wide range and only the highest-energy particles exceed $E_a$, even a small rise in average energy can noticeably increase that high-energy fraction, which is the main reason rate is so sensitive to temperature.
common_errors: Accepting that collision frequency alone could explain a large rate increase from a small temperature rise, without weighing how small that frequency effect actually is compared with the energy-fraction effect.

challenge_questions.statement:
Marble chips (CaCO₃) react with dilute hydrochloric acid. A student measures the volume of CO₂ gas produced every 30 seconds.
(a) Sketch the graph of volume of CO₂ (y-axis) against time (x-axis). Label the line. (2 marks)
(b) On the same axes, sketch and label the line you would expect if: (i) the acid were more concentrated, (ii) the marble chips were ground to a powder. (2 marks)
(c) Explain, using collision theory, why increasing concentration increases the rate. (3 marks)
(d) Explain why all three lines reach the same final volume. (1 mark)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) A curve that rises steeply at first then levels off to a plateau (horizontal line).
(b) (i) Steeper initial gradient, reaches the same final volume sooner. (ii) Also steeper — reaches the same final volume even more quickly.
(c) Higher concentration means more acid particles per unit volume. This increases the frequency of collisions between acid particles and marble chip particles per second. More frequent collisions mean more successful collisions per second, so the rate of reaction increases.
(d) The same total amount of marble and acid are used in each experiment, so the same total amount of CO₂ is produced. Only the speed of production changes, not the total amount.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly defines a successful (effective) collision?

options.text: Any collision between two reacting particles, regardless of their energy.
options.why_wrong: most collisions between reacting particles do not lead to a reaction; energy also matters, not just contact.

options.text: A collision in which the colliding particles have, between them, at least the activation energy needed to react.
A collision that happens at a high temperature.
options.why_wrong: temperature affects what fraction of collisions are successful, but a successful collision is defined by energy, not by the temperature of the sample as a whole.

options.text: A collision involving a catalyst particle.
options.why_wrong: successful collisions happen with or without a catalyst present; a catalyst only increases how many collisions meet the energy condition.

mcq.explanation: A successful collision is one where the particles' combined energy meets or exceeds the activation energy, allowing bonds to begin breaking.

mcq.stem: A fixed sample of gas is heated in a sealed, rigid container. Which statement correctly explains why its reaction rate increases?

options.text: Heating creates additional gas particles, increasing the amount reacting.
options.why_wrong: heating a fixed, sealed sample does not create new particles; the amount of gas present is unchanged.

options.text: Heating lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
options.why_wrong: temperature does not change the activation energy, which is a fixed property of the reaction pathway; only a catalyst changes activation energy.

options.text: Heating increases the particles' average kinetic energy, increasing the fraction of collisions with enough energy to succeed.
Heating has no real effect on rate unless a catalyst is also present.
options.why_wrong: temperature alone reliably increases rate, with or without any catalyst present.

mcq.explanation: The same fixed number of particles gain more kinetic energy on average when heated, increasing the proportion of collisions that exceed the activation energy.

mcq.stem: Which statement about catalysts is correct?

options.text: A catalyst changes the products of a reaction to ones that form more quickly.
options.why_wrong: the same products form whether or not a catalyst is used; only the rate at which they form changes.

options.text: A catalyst increases the overall energy released by an exothermic reaction.
options.why_wrong: the overall energy change, $\Delta H$, between reactants and products is unaffected by a catalyst; only the activation energy barrier changes.

options.text: A catalyst increases the frequency of collisions between reacting particles.
options.why_wrong: a catalyst's effect is on the energy barrier collisions must clear, not on how often particles collide.

options.text: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction without changing the products formed.

mcq.explanation: A catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy, increasing the fraction of successful collisions, without changing the products or the overall energy change.

mcq.stem: Powdered zinc reacts faster with dilute acid than an equal mass of zinc granules. Which explanation correctly accounts for this using collision theory?

options.text: The powdered zinc exposes more surface to the acid, increasing the frequency of collisions between acid and zinc particles.
The powdered zinc has a lower activation energy than the granules.
options.why_wrong: activation energy is a property of the reaction pathway between these particular reactants, not of the solid's physical form; it is the same for powder and granules.

options.text: The powdered zinc contains more zinc atoms than the same mass of granules.
options.why_wrong: the same mass of the same element contains the same number of atoms, whatever its physical form; the amount of zinc is unchanged.

options.text: The powdered zinc reacts at a higher temperature than the granules.
options.why_wrong: surface area affects rate independently of temperature; nothing in this scenario changes the temperature of either reaction.

mcq.explanation: Powdering the zinc exposes far more of its particles to the acid for the same total mass, increasing collision frequency and therefore rate, without changing activation energy, particle number or temperature.

flashcards.front: What is a successful (effective) collision?
flashcards.back: A collision in which the particles' combined kinetic energy is at least the activation energy, Ea, needed to start breaking reactant bonds.

flashcards.front: Why does raising temperature increase reaction rate?
flashcards.back: The same fixed number of particles gain more kinetic energy on average, so a larger fraction of collisions now exceed the activation energy and succeed.

flashcards.front: How does a catalyst's effect on activation energy differ from temperature's effect on rate?
flashcards.back: A catalyst lowers the activation energy itself, so more collisions succeed at the same temperature. Raising temperature leaves the activation energy unchanged but gives particles more energy, so more of them individually clear that same, unchanged bar.

flashcards.front: Does a catalyst change the products formed by a reaction?
flashcards.back: No. The same products form, and the overall energy change ($\Delta H$) is unchanged; a catalyst only lowers the activation energy, changing the rate, not the outcome.

flashcards.front: Crushing a solid reactant into powder, same total mass: what changes, and what stays the same, about its reaction rate and final product amount?
flashcards.back: Rate increases, because more surface is exposed, raising collision frequency. The final amount of product is unchanged, because the total mass of solid (the limiting reactant) has not changed.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any collision between reacting particles is enough to cause a reaction, provided there are enough collisions happening.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Everyday language uses 'collide' and 'react' almost interchangeably, and early particle-model teaching emphasises that particles are moving and bumping into each other without yet introducing an energy condition.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner explains an increase in rate purely by saying 'more collisions happen', without mentioning whether those extra collisions have enough energy to be successful.
misconceptions.correct_model: A collision only leads to a reaction if the colliding particles have, between them, at least as much kinetic energy as the activation energy, $E_a$, needed to start breaking bonds; the great majority of collisions in any reaction mixture do not meet this condition and the particles simply bounce apart unchanged.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the learner to estimate how many particle collisions happen in a beaker of reacting solution every second (a very large number) compared with how slowly some reactions visibly proceed, and ask what this mismatch implies about what fraction of collisions can possibly be successful.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A catalyst works by changing what products a reaction forms, which is why it 'helps' the reaction go.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners already associate 'helping a reaction happen' with producing something new, so a catalyst's role gets folded into the idea of making the reaction outcome different, rather than only making it faster.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that a catalysed and an uncatalysed version of the same reaction will give different products, or describes the catalyst as being 'part of the products'.
misconceptions.correct_model: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions become successful at the same temperature; it does not change the identity of the products or the overall energy change ($\Delta H$) of the reaction, only how quickly the same products are reached.
misconceptions.remediation: Show the same two reactants reacting with and without a catalyst, confirm (by a simple chemical test) that the same product forms in both cases, and ask what has changed if the products themselves have not.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Raising the temperature increases the number of particles present in a sample, which is why a hotter reaction mixture reacts faster.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners sometimes transfer the idea 'more of something causes more effect' from the concentration/surface-area factors (where more particles or more exposed particles genuinely are the cause) onto temperature, without separately considering what temperature actually changes.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner explains a temperature increase using language like 'there are more particles moving around', rather than 'the same particles are moving faster / have more energy'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Heating a fixed sample does not create new particles; it gives the same, fixed number of particles more kinetic energy on average. This increases the proportion of particles whose energy already exceeds the activation energy at any instant, which is the main reason a small temperature rise can noticeably increase rate; collision frequency also rises slightly because faster particles collide more often, but the energy effect is the dominant one.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the learner to state what quantity of reactant (in grams or moles) is present in a flask before and after it is heated; since this amount is unchanged, 'more particles' cannot be the explanation, which points back to particle speed/energy instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining a rate increase by saying only 'there are more collisions', without checking or stating whether those extra collisions also have enough energy to succeed.
common_mistakes.why: Collision frequency is the easier, more visual part of the explanation, so it is often given alone, leaving the energy condition implicit or missing.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always give both steps: first what happens to collision frequency or to particle energy, then explicitly connect that to the fraction or number of successful collisions.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing a catalyst as changing the products of a reaction, rather than only the rate at which the same products form.
common_mistakes.why: Learners associate anything that 'helps a reaction happen' with producing something different.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State explicitly that the same products and the same overall energy change ($\Delta H$) occur with or without the catalyst; only the activation energy and the rate differ.

common_mistakes.mistake: Attributing a temperature-driven rate increase to 'more particles' being present, rather than to the same particles having more energy.
common_mistakes.why: The 'more of something causes more effect' pattern transfers naturally from concentration and surface area, where it is correct, onto temperature, where it is not.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check the amount (in moles or grams) of reactant before and after heating; if it is unchanged, the explanation must be about energy, not about particle number.

exam_notes: A full collision-theory explanation always has two linked parts: what changes (frequency of collisions, or the particles' energy) and how that change affects the fraction or number of successful collisions; a one-part answer rarely earns full marks.
When explaining temperature's effect, state explicitly that the number of particles is unchanged and that it is their average energy that increases; examiners specifically credit this distinction.

When explaining a catalyst, state at least one quantity that stays the same (products, or the overall energy change) alongside the quantity that changes (the activation energy); naming only the activation energy is often an incomplete answer.

summary.big_idea: A reaction's rate depends on how often particles collide and on what fraction of those collisions clear the activation-energy barrier; every rate factor acts by changing one or both of these.
key_points: A successful collision needs at least the activation energy, Ea; most collisions fail this test and particles simply bounce apart.
Concentration, pressure and surface area increase rate by increasing collision frequency, without changing Ea or particle energy.
Temperature increases rate mainly by increasing particle energy, raising the fraction of collisions that clear the same Ea, not by creating more particles.
A catalyst increases rate by lowering Ea itself, without being used up and without changing the products or the overall energy change.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Every rate explanation needs two linked steps: what changes (frequency or energy), and how that changes the number of successful collisions.

exit_check.question: A reaction is sped up by adding a catalyst. State one thing that changes and one thing that stays exactly the same, and name the quantity responsible for each.
exit_check.answer: What changes: the activation energy, Ea, is lowered by the catalyst's alternative pathway, increasing the fraction of successful collisions. What stays the same: the products formed, and the overall energy change ($\Delta H$) of the reaction, which depend only on the reactants and products, not on the pathway taken between them.
