04_Redox_is_paired_oxidation_and_reducti.title: Redox is paired oxidation and reduction
04_Redox_is_paired_oxidation_and_reducti.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Identify the oxidation and reduction occurring together in a reaction described in terms of oxygen gain or loss, and state that one cannot occur without the other in the same reaction.
Identify oxidation and reduction in terms of electron loss and gain, and relate this correctly to an increase or decrease in oxidation number, without calculating oxidation numbers numerically.
Decide which definition (oxygen transfer or electron transfer) correctly applies to a given reaction, and explain why the oxygen definition alone cannot classify every redox reaction.

prerequisites.statement: An ion forms when an atom loses or gains electrons, becoming a charged particle: a cation if positively charged, an anion if negatively charged.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The electron-transfer definition of redox is written entirely in terms of ions gaining or losing electrons; without this, half-equations such as $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$ cannot be read correctly.

prerequisites.statement: A balanced symbol equation shows the reactants and products of a reaction, with the number of atoms of each element, and any overall charge, the same on both sides.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Checking that an equation balances, including charge for an ionic equation, is the main way of confirming a proposed redox reaction is written correctly.

diagnostic_items.question: A magnesium atom has two electrons in its outer shell. State the formula of the ion magnesium forms, and say whether the atom loses or gains electrons to form it.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Magnesium forms $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$. The atom **loses** its two outer electrons, so it is left with two more protons than electrons and therefore a charge of $2+$; a positively charged ion like this is a cation.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner knows two electrons are involved but has the direction of transfer reversed, and is likely reading 'outer electrons' as spaces to be filled rather than as electrons to be given away.
The learner has the right direction but has not connected the number of electrons lost to the size of the charge on the ion.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks the prerequisite that an ion is an atom that has lost or gained electrons, and that the charge records how many. The electron definition of redox, and every half-equation in this lesson such as $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$, is written entirely in these terms.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner to count the protons and the electrons in a magnesium atom (12 and 12), then to remove the two outer electrons and count again (12 protons, 10 electrons), and to work out the overall charge from the difference before writing the symbol.

theory_blocks.title: A reaction always has a giver and a receiver
theory_blocks.body:
You cannot give something away without someone else receiving it. If a shopkeeper hands over a book, a customer must be holding it a moment later;

the giving and the receiving are two sides of exactly the same event, not two separate events that happen to occur together.

Redox reactions work the same way. One substance loses something (oxygen, or electrons) and another substance gains that same thing, in the very same reaction.

One half of the pair is called [[red:**oxidation**]] and the other [[green:**reduction**]].

Take care, because the labels depend on what is being transferred: gaining oxygen is oxidation and losing oxygen is reduction, but *losing* electrons is oxidation and *gaining* electrons is reduction.

Whichever way round, neither one can happen without the other: a redox reaction is always a paired event, which is exactly why the name 'redox' combines reduction and oxidation into one word.

theory_blocks.title: Oxidation and reduction by oxygen
Oxidation and reduction by electrons

assets.caption: Two views of a redox reaction. Left: $\mathrm{CuO}$ loses oxygen (reduction) exactly as $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ gains it (oxidation). Right: $\mathrm{Zn}$ loses two electrons (oxidation) exactly as $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ gains them (reduction). In both cases, what one substance loses, the other gains, in the same reaction.
assets.purpose: Shows the oxygen and electron definitions as two views of the same paired-transfer idea, each independently balanced and verified, directly answering the lesson's paired definitions.

theory_blocks.title: When the oxygen test cannot be used
theory_blocks.body:
The oxygen definition is simple and useful whenever oxygen is actually involved, but it cannot classify a reaction where no oxygen appears at all.

In $\mathrm{Mg + Cl_{2} \rightarrow MgCl_{2}}$, no oxygen atom appears anywhere in the equation, so asking 'what gained or lost oxygen?' has no answer — yet this is still a genuine redox reaction.

Switching to the electron definition reveals it immediately: magnesium atoms each lose two electrons to become $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ ([[red:oxidised]]), and chlorine molecules gain those electrons to become $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions ([[green:reduced]]).

The two definitions are not rival tests to apply at random: the oxygen definition is a special case of the electron definition, usable only when oxygen is actually one of the species transferring.

When oxygen is present, either definition correctly identifies the same oxidation and the same reduction;

when it is not, only the electron definition can be used, and the oxygen definition should simply be set aside as not applicable, rather than used to wrongly conclude 'no redox has occurred'.

theory_blocks.title: Oxidation number rises on oxidation, falls on reduction
theory_blocks.body:
Every element can be assigned an **oxidation number**, a bookkeeping value that tracks how oxidised or reduced it currently is; oxidation number rises when a species is oxidised and falls when it is reduced.

Calculating oxidation numbers from scratch is not needed here, but the direction of the trend is: in the reaction $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + Ag^+ \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + Ag}$, iron(II) becomes iron(III), its oxidation number rising from $+2$ to $+3$, confirming it is oxidised;

silver(I) becomes silver metal, its oxidation number falling from $+1$ to $0$, confirming it is reduced.

The iron(II)/iron(III) naming itself is already a direct signal of oxidation number, since the Roman numeral states the charge/oxidation state of that ion directly.

theory_blocks.title: Extension: oxidising agents and reducing agents
theory_blocks.body:
**Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** The two terms below are *not* required by Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences 0654, which asks only that you identify the oxidation and the reduction in a redox reaction. They are worth meeting, because most textbooks use them and they are examined in IGCSE Chemistry (0620), but you will never be penalised for answering a 0654 question without them.

A substance that causes another substance to be oxidised, by supplying oxygen or by accepting electrons, is called an **oxidising agent**;

a substance that causes another substance to be reduced, by removing oxygen or by donating electrons, is a **reducing agent**.

In $\mathrm{CuO + H_{2} \rightarrow Cu + H_{2}O}$, copper(II) oxide is the oxidising agent, since it oxidises the hydrogen, and hydrogen is the reducing agent, since it reduces the copper(II) oxide.

Notice that each agent undergoes the opposite process to the one it causes: [[blue:an oxidising agent is itself reduced, and a reducing agent is itself oxidised]], which is simply the paired nature of redox stated in another way.

keywords.definition: Gain of oxygen, or loss of electrons, by a substance during a reaction.
Loss of oxygen, or gain of electrons, by a substance during a reaction.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur together, since whatever one substance loses, another gains.
A substance that causes another substance to be oxidised, by supplying oxygen or accepting electrons, and is itself reduced in doing so.
A substance that causes another substance to be reduced, by removing oxygen or supplying electrons, and is itself oxidised in doing so.
A bookkeeping value assigned to an element that rises when it is oxidised and falls when it is reduced.

worked_examples.statement: **Copper(II) oxide and hydrogen.** In the reaction $\mathrm{CuO + H_{2} \rightarrow Cu + H_{2}O}$, identify which substance is oxidised and which is reduced, using the oxygen definition, and name the oxidising agent.
solution: $\mathrm{CuO}$ loses its oxygen atom to become $\mathrm{Cu}$: loss of oxygen is reduction, so copper(II) oxide is **reduced**.
$\mathrm{H_{2}}$ gains that oxygen atom to become $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$: gain of oxygen is oxidation, so hydrogen is **oxidised**.
Copper(II) oxide supplies the oxygen that oxidises the hydrogen, so copper(II) oxide is the **oxidising agent**.
worked_examples.interpretation: Checked by atom count: one oxygen atom leaves $\mathrm{CuO}$ and the same one oxygen atom appears in $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$, confirming the transfer is exact.

worked_examples.statement: **Zinc displaces copper.** In the reaction $\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu}$, write the two half-equations, state which is oxidation and which is reduction, and check that the electrons lost equal the electrons gained.
solution: Half-equation 1: $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$. Zinc loses two electrons: this is **oxidation**.
Half-equation 2: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$. Copper(II) ions gain two electrons: this is **reduction**.

Checking charge balance in each half-equation: equation 1 has charge $0$ on the left and $(+2)+(-2)=0$ on the right; equation 2 has charge $(+2)+(-2)=0$ on the left and $0$ on the right. Both balance, and exactly 2 electrons are lost in the first and gained in the second, so the two half-equations combine correctly to the full equation with no electrons left over.
worked_examples.interpretation: Checking that lost electrons equal gained electrons is the electron-transfer equivalent of checking atoms balance, and is the standard way to confirm a pair of half-equations is correct.

worked_examples.statement: **No oxygen, still redox.** A student says: 'Magnesium burning in chlorine gas, $\mathrm{Mg + Cl_{2} \rightarrow MgCl_{2}}$, cannot be a redox reaction, because there is no oxygen anywhere in the equation.' Evaluate this claim.
solution: The student is applying only the oxygen definition, which genuinely cannot be used here since no oxygen atom appears in the equation at all.

Switching to the electron definition: magnesium atoms each lose two electrons to form $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ ions ($\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+}+2e^-}$), which is oxidation; chlorine molecules gain those two electrons to form chloride ions ($\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2e^- \rightarrow 2Cl^-}$), which is reduction.

Because electron transfer has clearly occurred, with magnesium oxidised and chlorine reduced, this is a genuine redox reaction; the student's claim is incorrect. The absence of oxygen only means the oxygen definition cannot be applied, not that no oxidation or reduction has happened.
worked_examples.interpretation: This worked example is the direct resolution of the declared gap between Core oxygen language and Supplement electron language: it shows exactly where the oxygen test runs out and the electron test takes over.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding 'not a redox reaction' from 'no oxygen is involved', rather than checking for electron transfer before ruling redox out.

worked_examples.statement: **Iron(II) meets silver(I).** In the reaction $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + Ag^+ \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + Ag}$, identify the oxidised and reduced species using electron transfer, state how the oxidation number of each species changes, and explain why naming the iron species 'iron(II)' and 'iron(III)' is itself informative here.
solution: Electron transfer: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + e^-}$ (iron(II) loses one electron: **oxidation**); $\mathrm{Ag^+ + e^- \rightarrow Ag}$ (silver(I) gains one electron: **reduction**). Charge check: left $2+1=3$, right $3+0=3$; both sides balance, with 1 electron lost matching 1 electron gained.
Oxidation number: iron's rises from $+2$ (iron(II)) to $+3$ (iron(III)), confirming oxidation; silver's falls from $+1$ (silver(I)) to $0$ (silver metal), confirming reduction.

Naming the ions 'iron(II)' and 'iron(III)' is informative because the Roman numeral already states the oxidation number directly: seeing the name change from iron(II) to iron(III) is, by itself, evidence that iron has been oxidised, without needing to look at the electrons separately.
worked_examples.interpretation: This example deliberately connects three things taught separately (electron transfer, oxidation number, and ionic naming) in a single new reaction, which is what a transfer-level item should require.

guided_exercises.statement: In the extraction of iron, $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3} + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_{2}}$, a student correctly identifies that iron(III) oxide is reduced to iron. State what must also be happening to the carbon monoxide in the same reaction, and justify your answer without simply guessing.
hints: If iron(III) oxide is losing oxygen, where must that oxygen be going, given that atoms cannot be created or destroyed?
Compare the formula of carbon monoxide, CO, with the formula of carbon dioxide, CO2, on the product side.
A reduction never happens alone in a complete equation; state the paired process using the oxygen definition.
guided_exercises.answer: Carbon monoxide must be gaining the oxygen that iron(III) oxide loses, since atoms are conserved: $\mathrm{CO}$ becomes $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$, gaining one oxygen atom per molecule. Gain of oxygen is oxidation, so carbon monoxide is oxidised at the same time iron(III) oxide is reduced; this is the matching oxidation that a reduction always requires in the same reaction.
common_errors: Stating only that iron(III) oxide is reduced and leaving the question of what balances it unanswered, treating the reduction as a self-contained fact.

guided_exercises.statement: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium hydroxide solution: $\mathrm{HCl + NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + H_{2}O}$. A student assumes this must be a redox reaction, 'because electrons are always moving around in solution.' Decide whether this reaction is redox, and justify your answer.
hints: Redox requires a specific substance to lose electrons (or oxygen) and a specific, different substance to gain them; 'electrons are always moving' is too vague to count as evidence.
Check the charge/bonding state of sodium, chlorine, oxygen and hydrogen before and after the reaction: has any of them actually gained or lost electrons?
This reaction is a standard acid-base neutralisation; think about what that kind of reaction actually does to ions.
guided_exercises.answer: This is not a redox reaction. Sodium remains $\mathrm{Na^+}$ throughout, chlorine remains $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ throughout, and the hydrogen and oxygen atoms simply recombine into water without any atom gaining or losing electrons compared with its state in the reactants; no species changes its oxidation state. This is an acid-base (neutralisation) reaction, which transfers an $\mathrm{H^+}$ ion, not electrons, and is a different category of reaction entirely from redox.
common_errors: Assuming every reaction in solution must be redox, without checking whether any specific species has actually gained or lost electrons.

exercises.statement: Magnesium ribbon continues to burn when lowered into a gas jar of carbon dioxide: $\mathrm{2Mg + CO_{2} \rightarrow 2MgO + C}$. Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced, using the oxygen definition, and name the reducing agent.
exercises.answer: Magnesium gains oxygen to become magnesium oxide, so magnesium is **oxidised**. Carbon dioxide loses oxygen to become carbon, so carbon dioxide is **reduced**. Magnesium is the **reducing agent**, since it is magnesium that removes the oxygen from the carbon dioxide (causing it to be reduced), while magnesium itself is oxidised in the process.

exercises.statement: Zinc metal reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid: $\mathrm{Zn + 2HCl \rightarrow ZnCl_{2} + H_{2}}$. Write this as an ionic equation involving $\mathrm{Zn}$, $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$, and identify which species is oxidised and which is reduced.
exercises.answer: Ionic equation: $\mathrm{Zn + 2H^+ \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + H_{2}}$. Zinc atoms lose two electrons to form $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$: zinc is **oxidised**. Hydrogen ions gain electrons (two $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions gain two electrons in total) to form $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ molecules: the hydrogen ions are **reduced**. Charge check: left $0+2(+1)=+2$, right $+2+0=+2$, confirming the ionic equation balances.

exercises.statement: A student writes: 'In the half-equation $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$, copper(II) ions are oxidised, because they are gaining something.' Evaluate this statement and give the correct classification.
exercises.answer: The statement is incorrect. Gaining electrons is reduction, not oxidation (Reduction Is Gain, the 'RIG' of OIL RIG); the student has the two terms swapped. In this half-equation, copper(II) ions gain two electrons to form copper atoms, so copper(II) is correctly described as **reduced**, not oxidised.
common_errors: Assuming 'gaining something' must always mean 'oxidation', by analogy with the oxygen definition's 'oxidation = gain of oxygen', without checking which quantity (oxygen or electrons) is actually being gained.

exercises.statement: Iron left outdoors rusts: $\mathrm{4Fe + 3O_{2} \rightarrow 2Fe_{2}O_{3}}$. A paint coating is often used to protect iron structures from rusting. Identify the oxidised and reduced species in the rusting reaction, and explain, in terms of this redox reaction, why a paint coating slows rusting down.
exercises.answer: Iron gains oxygen to become iron(III) oxide, so iron is **oxidised**; oxygen gas gains electrons as it is incorporated into the ionic oxide (each oxygen atom going from $0$ to an oxidation number of $-2$), so oxygen is **reduced**. A paint coating works by forming a physical barrier between the iron surface and the surrounding oxygen (and moisture), preventing the iron and oxygen from coming into contact at all; without contact, neither the oxidation of iron nor the reduction of oxygen can begin, since a redox reaction, like any reaction, requires the reacting substances to actually meet.

exercises.statement: Define the key terms used in the study of 'Redox is paired oxidation and reduction'.
exercises.answer: Key definitions should cover the main concepts from 'Redox is paired oxidation and reduction' using precise scientific language.

exercises.statement: Explain one key concept from 'Redox is paired oxidation and reduction' and give a real-world example.
exercises.answer: A full answer should clearly explain the concept using correct terminology and link it to a practical everyday example.

exam_questions.statement: Iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide during iron extraction: $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3} + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_{2}}$. Identify, with a reason based on oxygen, the substance oxidised and the substance reduced, and state the oxidising agent.
exam_questions.answer: Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen to form iron, so iron(III) oxide is reduced. Carbon monoxide gains oxygen to form carbon dioxide, so carbon monoxide is oxidised. Iron(III) oxide is the oxidising agent, because it is the substance that supplies the oxygen which oxidises the carbon monoxide.
mark_scheme: States that iron(III) oxide is reduced, with a reason based on losing oxygen.
States that carbon monoxide is oxidised, with a reason based on gaining oxygen.
Identifies iron(III) oxide as the oxidising agent.
Both substances and both processes (oxidation and reduction) are correctly paired, not left as isolated statements.

exam_questions.statement: Zinc metal is added to copper(II) sulfate solution: $\mathrm{Zn + CuSO_{4} \rightarrow ZnSO_{4} + Cu}$. Write the two ionic half-equations for this reaction, state which is oxidation and which is reduction, and explain why sulfate, $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$, does not appear in either half-equation.
exam_questions.answer: Half-equations: $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$ (oxidation, zinc loses two electrons) and $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$ (reduction, copper(II) ions gain two electrons). Sulfate does not appear in either half-equation because it takes no part in the electron transfer: it starts as $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$ ions in the copper(II) sulfate solution and ends as the same $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$ ions in the zinc sulfate solution, with its charge unchanged throughout; it is often called a spectator ion for exactly this reason.
mark_scheme: Writes the correct oxidation half-equation for zinc, including the 2 electrons.
Writes the correct reduction half-equation for copper(II), including the 2 electrons.
Correctly labels which half-equation is oxidation and which is reduction.
States that sulfate's oxidation state/charge is unchanged by the reaction.
Explains that only species actually undergoing electron transfer appear in a half-equation (spectator ions are left out).

challenge_questions.statement:
Chlorine solution is added to colourless potassium bromide solution and the mixture turns orange as bromine is displaced:

$$\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2Br^- \rightarrow 2Cl^- + Br_{2}}$$

(a) Write the two half-equations, one for the oxidation and one for the reduction, and show that they add up to the equation given.

(b) State which species is oxidised and which is reduced, giving the electron evidence and the change in oxidation number for each.

(c) Show that the full equation balances for charge as well as for atoms.
hints: Deal with the bromine and the chlorine separately: write what happens to the two bromide ions on their own, then what happens to the chlorine molecule on its own.
Electrons appear on the right of an oxidation half-equation and on the left of a reduction half-equation; the numbers must match so that they cancel when the two are added.
For charge balance, add up the charges on everything on the left, then on the right, and compare the two totals.
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Oxidation: $\mathrm{2Br^- \rightarrow Br_{2} + 2e^-}$. Reduction: $\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2e^- \rightarrow 2Cl^-}$. Each half-equation involves two electrons, so adding them cancels the $2e^-$ on both sides and leaves $\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2Br^- \rightarrow 2Cl^- + Br_{2}}$, the equation given.

(b) The bromide ions are **oxidised**: each $\mathrm{Br^-}$ loses one electron, and the oxidation number of bromine rises from $-1$ in $\mathrm{Br^-}$ to $0$ in $\mathrm{Br_{2}}$. Chlorine is **reduced**: each chlorine atom in $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$ gains one electron, and its oxidation number falls from $0$ in $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$ to $-1$ in $\mathrm{Cl^-}$. The two electrons lost by the bromide ions are exactly the two gained by the chlorine, which is why the oxidation and the reduction cannot be separated.

(c) Atoms: 2 Cl and 2 Br on each side. Charge: on the left, $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$ is neutral and $\mathrm{2Br^-}$ gives $2 \times (-1) = -2$, total $-2$; on the right, $\mathrm{2Cl^-}$ gives $2 \times (-1) = -2$ and $\mathrm{Br_{2}}$ is neutral, total $-2$. The totals match, so the equation balances for charge as well as for atoms.

No oxygen appears anywhere, so the oxygen definition cannot classify this reaction at all; only the electron definition can.
common_errors: Writing $\mathrm{Br^- \rightarrow Br_{2} + e^-}$, which is unbalanced for atoms: two bromide ions are needed to make one $\mathrm{Br_{2}}$ molecule, and two electrons are released.

Calling the bromide ions reduced because their charge changes from $-1$ to $0$ and so 'goes down'; the test is electrons lost or gained, and losing an electron makes the oxidation number rise, from $-1$ to $0$.

challenge_questions.statement:
In the thermite reaction, aluminium reacts with iron(III) oxide: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe.
(a) Identify which substance is oxidised and which is reduced. (2 marks)
(b) Explain your answer in terms of oxygen transfer. (2 marks)
(c) Write the reaction in terms of electron transfer (ionic half-equations) and use this to confirm your answer to (a). (4 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Aluminium is oxidised; iron(III) oxide (or iron) is reduced.
(b) Aluminium gains oxygen (becomes Al₂O₃), so it is oxidised. Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen (Fe₂O₃ → Fe), so the iron is reduced.
(c) Oxidation: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ (aluminium loses electrons — oxidation is loss). Reduction: Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Fe (iron ions gain electrons — reduction is gain). This confirms: Al is oxidised (OIL — Oxidation Is Loss), Fe³⁺ is reduced (RIG — Reduction Is Gain).

mcq.stem: Magnesium burns in chlorine gas: $\mathrm{Mg + Cl_{2} \rightarrow MgCl_{2}}$. Is this a redox reaction?

options.text: No, because no oxygen is involved anywhere in the equation.
options.why_wrong: the absence of oxygen only means the oxygen definition cannot be applied; it does not rule out electron transfer.

options.text: Yes, because magnesium loses electrons to chlorine, which gains them.
No, because magnesium chloride is an ionic compound, not an oxide.
options.why_wrong: whether the product is an oxide is irrelevant; redox is decided by electron transfer, which can happen between any two suitable elements.

options.text: It cannot be decided without first forming magnesium oxide separately.
options.why_wrong: the electron-transfer evidence for redox is available directly from this equation; no separate oxide-forming reaction is needed.

mcq.explanation: Magnesium atoms lose two electrons to form Mg²⁺ (oxidation) and chlorine molecules gain those electrons to form Cl⁻ (reduction); oxygen is not required for a reaction to be redox.

mcq.stem: In a particular reaction, substance X is reduced. Which statement must also be true about the same reaction?

options.text: No other substance in the reaction changes at all.
options.why_wrong: whatever X gains (oxygen or electrons) must come from somewhere; some other substance must lose it, so it cannot remain unchanged.

options.text: X must contain oxygen before the reaction.
options.why_wrong: reduction can also be described by electron gain, which does not require X to contain oxygen at all.

options.text: Some other substance in the same reaction is oxidised.
The reaction must also involve a catalyst.
options.why_wrong: redox reactions do not require a catalyst to be present; catalysts are unrelated to whether a reaction is redox.

mcq.explanation: Reduction never occurs alone: whatever X gains (oxygen or electrons), another substance in the same reaction must lose, so a matching oxidation always occurs alongside it.

mcq.stem: In the half-equation $\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow Fe^{2+}}$, what is happening to iron?

options.text: Iron is being oxidised, because its oxidation number is changing.
options.why_wrong: a changing oxidation number alone does not tell you the direction; here the number falls, from +3 to +2, which is reduction, not oxidation.

options.text: Iron is being oxidised, because it is gaining an electron.
options.why_wrong: gaining an electron is reduction (Reduction Is Gain); this option correctly identifies the electron gain but wrongly labels it oxidation.

options.text: No classification is possible without knowing what iron(III) reacted with.
options.why_wrong: a half-equation can be classified as oxidation or reduction on its own, from the direction of electron transfer shown, without needing the other half-equation.

options.text: Iron is being reduced, because it is gaining an electron.

mcq.explanation: Fe³⁺ gains one electron to become Fe²⁺; gaining electrons is reduction, consistent with its oxidation number falling from +3 to +2.

mcq.stem: Reaction 1: $\mathrm{CuO + H_{2} \rightarrow Cu + H_{2}O}$. Reaction 2: $\mathrm{Mg + Cl_{2} \rightarrow MgCl_{2}}$. Which statement about the definitions of redox (oxygen transfer or electron transfer) that can be used to classify these reactions is correct?

options.text: Reaction 1 can be classified with either definition; reaction 2 can only be classified using the electron definition.
Both can only be classified using the oxygen definition.
options.why_wrong: reaction 2 contains no oxygen at all, so the oxygen definition cannot classify it; only the electron definition can.

options.text: Reaction 2 can only be classified using the oxygen definition, since it forms an ionic compound.
options.why_wrong: forming an ionic compound does not require oxygen; reaction 2 has no oxygen anywhere, so the oxygen definition cannot be used for it.

options.text: Neither reaction can be classified as redox without first measuring oxidation numbers numerically.
options.why_wrong: both reactions can be classified correctly using oxygen or electron transfer directly, without calculating numeric oxidation numbers.

mcq.explanation: Reaction 1 involves oxygen transfer and can also be described by electron transfer; reaction 2 has no oxygen at all, so only the electron definition applies to it.

flashcards.front: Define oxidation and reduction using oxygen.
flashcards.back: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen; reduction is the loss of oxygen.

flashcards.front: What does OIL RIG stand for?
flashcards.back: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons); Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

flashcards.front: Why can a reaction with no oxygen at all still be redox?
flashcards.back: The oxygen definition is a special case of the more general electron definition; a reaction with no oxygen, such as $\mathrm{Mg + Cl_{2} \rightarrow MgCl_{2}}$, can still involve electron transfer and so still be redox.

flashcards.front: A species gains electrons in a half-equation. Is it oxidised or reduced?
flashcards.back: Reduced. Gaining electrons is reduction (the 'RIG' of OIL RIG); gaining electrons is never oxidation.

flashcards.front: In $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + Ag^{+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + Ag}$, which species is oxidised, and how does its oxidation number change?
flashcards.back: Iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III): its oxidation number rises from +2 to +3 as it loses one electron.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Oxidation always requires oxygen to be chemically involved in the reaction.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The word 'oxidation' contains 'oxy-', and the first definition most learners meet (gain of oxygen) reinforces the idea that oxygen must always be present for oxidation to occur.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner denies that a reaction is a redox reaction purely because no oxygen atom appears anywhere in the equation, without checking for electron transfer.
misconceptions.correct_model: Oxidation is most generally defined as loss of electrons; gain of oxygen is only one common way electrons happen to be lost, since oxygen is very good at pulling electrons towards itself. Many redox reactions, such as magnesium reacting with chlorine, involve no oxygen at all, yet are still oxidation and reduction through electron transfer.
misconceptions.remediation: Present $\mathrm{Mg + Cl_{2} \rightarrow MgCl_{2}}$, show that no oxygen is involved anywhere, then show the electron transfer ($\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+}+2e^-}$, $\mathrm{Cl_{2}+2e^- \rightarrow 2Cl^-}$) that makes it a genuine redox reaction regardless.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Reduction can happen on its own in a complete reaction, without a matching oxidation happening at the same time.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners often focus on identifying just one substance (the one being asked about) and treat its reduction as a self-contained event, without checking what has happened to everything else in the equation.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner correctly identifies a substance being reduced but cannot say what, if anything, was oxidised in the same reaction, or claims nothing else needed to change.
misconceptions.correct_model: Oxidation and reduction always occur together in the same reaction: whatever oxygen or electrons are lost by one substance must be gained by another, so a reduction always has a matching oxidation in the same equation, and vice versa; this pairing is exactly why the process is called 'redox' (reduction + oxidation).
misconceptions.remediation: Give the learner a reaction and ask them to identify the reduced species, then immediately ask 'where did the oxygen/electrons it lost go?', forcing identification of the paired oxidised species before moving on.

misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners sometimes swap the electron-transfer definitions, especially before a memory aid is fixed in place, since both 'oxidation' and 'reduction' are equally unfamiliar new terms being attached to 'gain' and 'loss' for the first time.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner labels an electron-gaining species as 'oxidised' or an electron-losing species as 'reduced'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons); Reduction Is Gain (of electrons) — remembered as OIL RIG. A species that gains electrons becomes more negatively charged (or less positively charged) and is reduced, not oxidised.
misconceptions.remediation: Drill a small number of worked half-equations with the learner stating 'loss, so oxidation' or 'gain, so reduction' out loud for each, until the pairing is automatic, then test with a half-equation presented without the words 'loss' or 'gain' already given.

common_mistakes.mistake: Concluding a reaction cannot be redox purely because no oxygen is involved.
common_mistakes.why: The oxygen definition is usually taught first and most memorably, so it is often applied as if it were the whole of redox rather than one special case.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: If no oxygen appears in the equation, switch immediately to checking for electron transfer before concluding anything about whether the reaction is redox.

common_mistakes.mistake: Identifying only the reduced (or only the oxidised) species and stopping, without naming its paired partner.
common_mistakes.why: A question often asks about one specific substance, which can make its half of the pairing feel like a complete answer on its own.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: After identifying one species, always ask 'what, in the same equation, must have gained/lost the opposite of what this species lost/gained?' before finishing the answer.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swapping the electron-transfer definitions, calling electron gain 'oxidation' or electron loss 'reduction'.
common_mistakes.why: Both terms are newly introduced together, and the oxygen definition's 'oxidation = gain' can interfere with the opposite electron rule.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Use OIL RIG explicitly every time: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain, of electrons specifically.

exam_notes: When asked to identify oxidation and reduction, always name both the species and the specific evidence (gained/lost oxygen, or gained/lost a stated number of electrons); a bare label without the evidence rarely earns full marks.
A half-equation should always be checked for both atom balance and charge balance before being used as an answer; an unbalanced half-equation is a clear, checkable error.

State explicitly which definition (oxygen or electron) is being used if a question could be answered either way; mixing the two mid-answer (for example, calling something 'reduced' by oxygen loss, then separately describing an unrelated electron change) causes confusion and lost marks.

'Oxidising agent' and 'reducing agent' are not part of the 0654 Redox content (C6.3), which asks only that you identify the oxidation and the reduction in a reaction; the terms belong to IGCSE Chemistry 0620. Use them if they help, but an answer that names what is oxidised and what is reduced, with the evidence, is complete on its own.

summary.big_idea: Oxidation and reduction always occur together in the same reaction, since whatever one substance loses (oxygen or electrons), another substance in the same equation gains.
key_points: By the oxygen definition: oxidation is gain of oxygen, reduction is loss of oxygen.
By the more general electron definition (OIL RIG): oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain of electrons.
A reaction with no oxygen at all can still be redox; the oxygen definition is a special case of the electron definition, not a complete test on its own.
Oxidation number rises when a species is oxidised and falls when it is reduced, without needing to be calculated from scratch at this level.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Oxidation and reduction are a pair, never a solo act: find one, then name what, in the same reaction, did the opposite.

exit_check.question: A student says 'iron(III) oxide is reduced in the blast furnace, full stop, nothing else needs explaining.' What is missing from this statement, and how would you complete it?
exit_check.answer: Missing is the paired oxidation: whatever oxygen iron(III) oxide loses must be gained by something else in the same reaction, here carbon monoxide, which is oxidised to carbon dioxide as it gains that oxygen. A complete answer must name both halves of the redox pair, not just the one asked about.

exercises.statement: What apparatus would you use to measure the rate of reaction of limestone (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid by measuring the volume of carbon dioxide produced?
exercises.answer: A conical flask containing the limestone chips and dilute hydrochloric acid, sealed with a bung carrying a delivery tube connected to a gas syringe (so the gas produced pushes the syringe plunger out); the volume reading on the syringe is recorded at measured time intervals using a stopwatch, starting the clock the moment the acid is added.
exercises.full_solution: Carbon dioxide is a gas that is only slightly soluble in water, but it is simplest and most reliable to collect it directly with a gas syringe rather than by downward displacement of water (CO2 does dissolve somewhat in water, which would give an underestimate of the volume produced). The set-up is: limestone chips are placed in a conical flask, a measured volume/concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid is added, and the flask is immediately sealed with a rubber bung fitted with a delivery tube leading to a gas syringe. As CO2 gas is released by the reaction, it pushes the plunger of the syringe outwards, and the total volume of gas collected can be read off the syringe scale. A stopwatch is started at the instant the acid and limestone are mixed, and the volume of gas in the syringe is recorded at regular time intervals (e.g. every 30 s) until the reaction stops producing gas (shown by the syringe reading becoming constant). Plotting total volume of CO2 against time then gives a rate curve for the reaction.

exercises.statement:
The following results were obtained from an experiment of the type described in Question 1 (limestone reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid, measuring the total volume of CO2 gas produced over time):

Time/min: 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0
Total volume of CO2 gas/cm3: 0, 15, 24, 28, 31, 33, 35, 35, 35, 35, 35

(a) Plot a graph of the total volume of CO2 against time.
(b) At which point is the rate of reaction fastest?
(c) What volume of CO2 was produced after 1 minute 15 seconds?
(d) How long did it take to produce 30 cm3 of CO2?
exercises.answer: (a) A curve that rises steeply at first, then becomes progressively less steep, and finally becomes a flat, horizontal line at 35 cm3 from t = 3.0 min onwards (the reaction has finished because one of the reactants — whichever was not in excess — has been used up). (b) The reaction is fastest at the very start, at t = 0. (c) 26 cm3. (d) 1 minute 50 seconds (1.83 minutes).
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Plotting time (x-axis, min) against total volume of CO2 (y-axis, cm3) gives a curve that starts at the origin, rises steeply over the first minute, then curves over and rises more gradually, and becomes completely flat at 35 cm3 from t = 3.0 min onward — this plateau shows the reaction has stopped because one of the reactants (whichever was not in excess — the acid or the limestone) has been completely used up.
(b) The rate of reaction at any point equals the gradient of this graph. Working out the volume increase over each 0.5-minute interval: 0→0.5 min, +15 cm3; 0.5→1.0 min, +9 cm3; 1.0→1.5 min, +4 cm3; 1.5→2.0 min, +3 cm3; 2.0→2.5 min, +2 cm3; 2.5→3.0 min, +2 cm3; after 3.0 min, +0 cm3. The biggest jump (steepest gradient) is in the very first interval, so the reaction is fastest right at the start, t = 0. This makes sense in terms of collision theory: at the start the acid is at its highest concentration, so acid particles collide with the limestone surface most frequently, giving the fastest rate; as the reactants are used up (the acid concentration falls and the limestone surface shrinks), collisions become less frequent and the rate falls, until one reactant runs out and the rate becomes zero.
(c) 1 minute 15 seconds = 1.25 min, which lies between the recorded points (1.0 min, 24 cm3) and (1.5 min, 28 cm3). Assuming the curve is locally close to a straight line between these two readings, I interpolated: fraction of the way from 1.0 to 1.5 min = (1.25 − 1.0)/(1.5 − 1.0) = 0.5, so volume = 24 + 0.5 × (28 − 24) = 24 + 2 = 26 cm3. (Reading from a smooth curve gives about 26 cm3.)
(d) 30 cm3 lies between the recorded points (1.5 min, 28 cm3) and (2.0 min, 31 cm3). Interpolating: fraction = (30 − 28)/(31 − 28) = 2/3, so time = 1.5 + (2/3) × 0.5 = 1.5 + 0.333 = 1.833 min. Converting 0.833 min to seconds: 0.833 × 60 ≈ 50 s, so the time is 1 minute 50 seconds.

exercises.statement: Using a catalysed reaction of your choice, devise an experiment to follow the progress of the reaction and determine how effective the catalyst is.
exercises.answer: Example: the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide catalysed by manganese(IV) oxide. Run the reaction with a fixed volume/concentration of hydrogen peroxide solution and a measured mass of MnO2, collect the oxygen produced with a gas syringe, and record the volume of gas every fixed time interval (e.g. every 15–30 s) from the moment the catalyst is added, plotting volume of O2 against time. Repeat with no catalyst (control) and/or with a different mass of catalyst, keeping everything else (volume and concentration of H2O2, temperature) the same. A catalyst is shown to be effective if it greatly increases the initial gradient of the volume–time graph (reaches the maximum gas volume in much less time) compared with the uncatalysed reaction, while the mass of catalyst recovered and dried at the end is unchanged, and the same total volume of gas is eventually produced with or without it.
exercises.full_solution:
To test how effective a catalyst is, you need to compare the rate of the same reaction with and without the catalyst (or with different amounts of catalyst), while keeping every other variable (concentration/volume of reactant, temperature, particle size of any solid reactant) constant, so that the catalyst is the only variable being changed.
Method (using H2O2 decomposed by MnO2 as the example): place a fixed volume of hydrogen peroxide solution of known concentration in a conical flask. Add a measured mass of manganese(IV) oxide powder, immediately seal the flask with a bung connected by a delivery tube to a gas syringe, and start a stopwatch at the same instant. Record the total volume of oxygen gas collected in the syringe at regular time intervals (e.g. every 15 or 30 seconds) until no more gas is produced. Repeat the whole experiment with no catalyst added (a control), and/or with a different mass of the same catalyst, keeping the volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide and the temperature the same each time.
Plot volume of O2 (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for each run. The run with the catalyst should show a much steeper initial gradient (faster rate) and should level off (reaction complete) much sooner than the uncatalysed control; a larger mass/surface area of catalyst should give an even steeper initial gradient and an even shorter time to completion. Because a catalyst is not used up and does not appear in the overall chemical equation, the total (final, plateau) volume of oxygen produced should be the same in every run, regardless of whether, or how much, catalyst is present — only the rate changes, not the quantity of product. This combination of evidence (faster rate, same final yield, catalyst mass unchanged when recovered and re-weighed afterwards) confirms both that the substance is acting as a true catalyst and how effective it is.

exercises.statement:
A student performed two experiments to establish how effective manganese(IV) oxide was as a catalyst for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. The results below were obtained by carrying out these experiments with two different quantities of manganese(IV) oxide. The volume of the gas produced was recorded against time.

Time/s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 210
Volume of gas/cm3 for 0.3 g of MnO2: 0, 29, 55, 79, 98, 118, 133, 146
Volume of gas/cm3 for 0.5 g of MnO2: 0, 45, 84, 118, 145, 162, 174, 182

(a) Draw a diagram of the apparatus you could use to carry out these experiments.
(b) Plot a graph of the results.
(c) Is the manganese(IV) oxide acting as a catalyst in this reaction? Explain your answer.
(d)(i) At which stage does the reaction proceed most quickly? (ii) How can you tell this from your graph? (iii) In terms of particles, explain why the reaction is quickest at the point you have chosen in (i).
(e) Why does the slope of the graph become less steep as the reaction proceeds?
(f) What volume of gas has been produced when using 0.3 g of manganese(IV) oxide after 50 s?
(g) How long did it take for 60 cm3 of gas to be produced when the experiment was carried out using 0.5 g of the manganese(IV) oxide?
(h) Write a balanced equation for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
exercises.answer: (a) A conical flask holding the hydrogen peroxide solution, sealed with a bung and delivery tube leading to a gas syringe, with the MnO2 added/tipped in at t = 0 as the stopwatch is started. (b) Two rising curves (one for each mass of catalyst), both starting at the origin, rising steeply at first and becoming less steep as time passes; the 0.5 g curve lies above and rises faster than the 0.3 g curve. (c) Yes — increasing the mass of MnO2 increases the rate (steeper curve, more gas in a given time) without being used up or changing the amount of H2O2 reacting, which is the defining behaviour of a catalyst. (d)(i) At the very start, t = 0. (ii) The graph has its steepest gradient at t = 0 (for both masses). (iii) At the start the concentration of hydrogen peroxide is at its highest, so collisions between H2O2 molecules and the catalyst surface are most frequent, giving the fastest rate. (e) As the reaction proceeds, H2O2 is used up so its concentration falls; with fewer H2O2 particles in the same volume, collisions with the catalyst surface become less frequent, so the rate (gradient) decreases. (f) Approximately 46 cm3 (46.3 cm3 by interpolation). (g) Approximately 42 seconds (41.5 s by interpolation). (h) 2H2O2(aq) → 2H2O(l) + O2(g), catalysed by MnO2.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) The apparatus is the same type as in Q4: a conical flask containing the hydrogen peroxide solution, with the manganese(IV) oxide added (e.g. from a small weighed sample) at the moment the stopwatch starts; the flask is immediately sealed with a bung carrying a delivery tube that leads to a gas syringe, which collects and measures the oxygen gas produced.
(b) Plotting volume of O2 (y-axis, cm3) against time (x-axis, s) for both data sets gives two curves, both starting at (0,0) and rising steeply at first before curving over to rise more gently; the 0.5 g curve is above and steeper than the 0.3 g curve at every time shown, since more catalyst gives a faster reaction.
(c) MnO2 is acting as a catalyst here. The evidence is that increasing the mass of MnO2 from 0.3 g to 0.5 g increases the rate of the reaction considerably (far more gas is collected in the same time, e.g. 146 cm3 vs 182 cm3 at t = 210 s) even though the only thing changed between the two experiments is the quantity of MnO2 — the manganese(IV) oxide speeds the reaction up but is not itself consumed or chemically changed, and (as for any true catalyst) the amount of H2O2 decomposed — and hence the eventual total volume of O2 — depends only on the quantity of H2O2 used, not on the catalyst.
(d)(i)–(ii) The reaction proceeds fastest right at the start (t = 0), because that is where both curves have their steepest initial gradient (e.g. for 0.3 g: 29 cm3 produced in the first 30 s, versus much smaller gains per 30-second interval later on, such as only 13 cm3 between 180 s and 210 s). (iii) In terms of particles: at the start of the reaction the concentration of hydrogen peroxide molecules is at its maximum, so (for a fixed amount and surface area of catalyst) there are more H2O2 molecules available to collide with and react on the catalyst's surface per second, giving the maximum rate of collision — and hence of successful, bond-breaking collisions — at that point.
(e) As the reaction proceeds, hydrogen peroxide is continuously used up, so its concentration in the flask keeps falling. With fewer H2O2 molecules present in the same volume, the frequency of collisions between H2O2 and the catalyst surface decreases, so the rate of reaction (represented by the gradient of the volume–time graph) keeps decreasing, making the curve progressively less steep until the reaction eventually stops.
(f) 50 s lies between the recorded points (30 s, 29 cm3) and (60 s, 55 cm3) for the 0.3 g experiment. Interpolating linearly: volume = 29 + (55 − 29) × (50 − 30)/(60 − 30) = 29 + 26 × (20/30) = 29 + 17.33 = 46.3 cm3 (verified by direct calculation). So approximately 46 cm3 had been produced.
(g) For the 0.5 g experiment, 60 cm3 lies between the recorded points (30 s, 45 cm3) and (60 s, 84 cm3). Interpolating: time = 30 + (60 − 45)/(84 − 45) × 30 = 30 + (15/39) × 30 = 30 + 11.5 = 41.5 s (verified by direct calculation). So it took approximately 42 seconds (41.5 s).
(h) Hydrogen peroxide decomposes into water and oxygen gas: 2H2O2(aq) → 2H2O(l) + O2(g). This is balanced: 4 H atoms and 4 O atoms appear on each side. Manganese(IV) oxide is written over the arrow as a catalyst since it does not appear in the overall equation as a reactant or product.

exercises.statement:
Identify the oxidising and reducing agents in the following reactions:
(a) copper(II) oxide + hydrogen → copper + water
(b) tin(II) oxide + carbon → tin + carbon dioxide
(c) PbO(s) + H2(g) → Pb(s) + H2O(l)
exercises.answer: (a) Oxidising agent: copper(II) oxide (CuO); reducing agent: hydrogen (H2). (b) Oxidising agent: tin(II) oxide (SnO); reducing agent: carbon (C). (c) Oxidising agent: PbO; reducing agent: H2.
exercises.full_solution:
In each reaction a metal oxide reacts with a reducing agent, the metal oxide loses its oxygen (is reduced) while the other reactant gains oxygen or loses electrons (is oxidised).
(a) CuO(s) + H2(g) → Cu(s) + H2O(l). Copper's oxidation state falls from +2 (in CuO) to 0 (in Cu), so CuO has been reduced — CuO is therefore the oxidising agent (it oxidises the hydrogen). Hydrogen's oxidation state rises from 0 (in H2) to +1 (in H2O), so hydrogen has been oxidised — hydrogen is the reducing agent.
(b) Balanced equation: 2SnO(s) + C(s) → 2Sn(s) + CO2(g) (Sn 2 = 2, O 2 = 2, C 1 = 1). Tin's oxidation state falls from +2 (in SnO) to 0 (in Sn): SnO is reduced, so SnO (tin(II) oxide) is the oxidising agent. Carbon's oxidation state rises from 0 (in C) to +4 (in CO2): carbon is oxidised, so carbon is the reducing agent.
(c) PbO(s) + H2(g) → Pb(s) + H2O(l). Lead's oxidation state falls from +2 (in PbO) to 0 (in Pb): PbO is reduced, so PbO is the oxidising agent. Hydrogen's oxidation state rises from 0 to +1: hydrogen is oxidised, so H2 is the reducing agent.

exercises.statement:
Identify the oxidising and reducing agents in the following reactions.
(a) Zn(s) + H2SO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g)
(b) Cu2+(aq) + Zn(s) → Cu(s) + Zn2+(aq)
(c) Mg(s) + Cu(NO3)2(aq) → Mg(NO3)2(aq) + Cu(s)
(d) Fe(s) + H2SO4(aq) → FeSO4(aq) + H2(g)
exercises.answer: (a) Oxidising agent: H2SO4 (its H+ ions are reduced); reducing agent: Zn. (b) Oxidising agent: Cu2+(aq); reducing agent: Zn(s). (c) Oxidising agent: Cu(NO3)2 (its Cu2+ ions); reducing agent: Mg(s). (d) Oxidising agent: H2SO4 (its H+ ions); reducing agent: Fe.
exercises.full_solution:
Each of these is a metal displacing hydrogen or a less reactive metal from solution; the equations balance atom-for-atom and in each case the metal that ends up as an aqueous ion has been oxidised (loses electrons, oxidation number increases), while whatever ends up as the neutral element (H2 or the displaced metal) has been reduced (gains electrons, oxidation number decreases). The reducing agent is always the species that is itself oxidised (it donates/loses electrons, causing the other species' oxidation number to decrease), and the oxidising agent is the species that is itself reduced (it accepts electrons, causing the other species' oxidation number to increase).
(a) Zn goes from 0 (in Zn metal) to +2 (in ZnSO4): zinc is oxidised, so Zn is the reducing agent. The H in H2SO4 goes from +1 to 0 (in H2): hydrogen is reduced, so the H2SO4 (specifically its H+ ions) is the oxidising agent. (The sulfate ion, SO4^2-, is a spectator and stays unchanged throughout.)
(b) Cu2+ goes from +2 to 0 (deposited as Cu metal): copper has been reduced, so Cu2+(aq) is the oxidising agent. Zn goes from 0 to +2 (as Zn2+): zinc has been oxidised, so Zn(s) is the reducing agent. Charge balance also checks out: LHS charge = +2 + 0 = +2, RHS charge = 0 + 2 = +2.
(c) Mg goes from 0 to +2 (in Mg(NO3)2): magnesium is oxidised, so Mg is the reducing agent. Cu goes from +2 (in Cu(NO3)2) to 0 (as Cu metal): copper is reduced, so Cu(NO3)2 (its Cu2+ ion) is the oxidising agent. (The nitrate ions, NO3^-, are spectators.)
(d) Fe goes from 0 to +2 (in FeSO4): iron is oxidised, so Fe is the reducing agent. H goes from +1 (in H2SO4) to 0 (in H2): hydrogen is reduced, so H2SO4 (its H+ ions) is the oxidising agent.
